label: The MOSFET as a switch
prereqs: Logical connectives: AND, OR, NOT, IMPLIES
lesson:
# The MOSFET as a switch

Before a tool can time, size or characterize a gate, it needs the simplest faithful picture of a transistor: a switch controlled by its gate voltage. The switch model is what switch-level simulators, logic extractors and netlist checkers run on, and it is the first thing a designer reasons with when drawing a new cell. Knowing exactly where the model is right, and where it breaks, tells you which questions it can answer and which need resistance, capacitance and thresholds.

## Gate voltage opens and closes the channel

An nMOS conducts when its gate is high and is open when its gate is low. A pMOS is the complement: it conducts when its gate is low. In circuit terms, the device turns on when its gate-to-source voltage passes the threshold $V_t$, and in a gate the nMOS sources sit near ground and the pMOS sources near $V_{DD}$, so "high" and "low" are measured against those rails. A gate input therefore drives a pair of opposite switches: when input A is 1, every nMOS it controls is closed and every pMOS it controls is open. That single fact is what makes complementary logic work, and it is why a CMOS gate input looks to the driver like a capacitor rather than a resistor: no DC current flows into a gate.

## Series means AND, parallel means OR

Switches compose. Two switches in series conduct only if both are closed; two in parallel conduct if either is. For nMOS devices with gates A and B, a series pair conducts on $AB$ and a parallel pair on $A + B$. For pMOS devices the same topology conducts on the complemented inputs: a series pair on $\bar A \bar B$ and a parallel pair on $\bar A + \bar B$. A static CMOS gate puts an nMOS network between the output and ground and a pMOS network between $V_{DD}$ and the output, built so that for every input vector exactly one network conducts. Example: two series nMOS from Y to ground with two parallel pMOS from $V_{DD}$ to Y pull Y low exactly when $AB = 1$, and high otherwise, which is a NAND2.

## Where the switch model stops

The ideal switch has no resistance, no capacitance and no threshold loss, so it predicts logic values but never delay or power. Two refinements recover most of what tools need. First, strengths: an nMOS passes a strong 0 but only a weak 1, rising to $V_{DD} - V_{tn}$, and a pMOS passes a strong 1 but a weak 0. Switch-level simulators track strong, weak and undriven levels so they can flag degraded nodes. Second, charge storage: a node driven by neither network keeps its value on its capacitance for a while, a state such simulators model explicitly. For timing, the next step up replaces each closed switch by an effective resistance and each node by a capacitance, which is the RC model.

## Going deeper

Weste and Harris, "CMOS VLSI Design: A Circuits and Systems Perspective" (4th ed.), chapter 1; Bryant's work on switch-level simulation (the MOSSIM simulators).

problems.q:
In the switch model of a MOSFET, when does an nMOS conduct?

A) Whenever its drain is above its source

B) When its gate is high

C) When its gate is low

D) When its source is high
problems.a: When its gate is high
problems.e: An nMOS turns on when its gate-source voltage exceeds the threshold, which for a source near ground means a high gate.

problems.q:
Why do static CMOS pull-down networks use nMOS and pull-up networks use pMOS, not the other way round?

A) pMOS cannot be placed in series

B) nMOS is always faster, so it goes where speed matters

C) nMOS leaks less, so it goes nearest ground

D) nMOS passes a strong 0 and pMOS passes a strong 1
problems.a: nMOS passes a strong 0 and pMOS passes a strong 1
problems.e: An nMOS discharging a node stays on all the way to 0 V; a pMOS charging a node stays on all the way to VDD. The reverse placements give threshold-degraded levels.

B) Whenever its drain is above its source

C) When its gate is low

D) When its gate is high
problems.a: When its gate is high
problems.e: An nMOS turns on when its gate-source voltage exceeds the threshold, which for a source near ground means a high gate.

problems.q:
Why is the switch model not enough to compute a gate's delay?

A) It assumes the wrong polarity for pMOS

B) It ignores the on-resistance and the capacitances the transistors charge

C) It ignores the logic function

D) It cannot represent series connections
problems.a: It ignores the on-resistance and the capacitances the transistors charge
problems.e: The switch model says which paths conduct, not how fast. Delay needs each conducting device's effective resistance and the capacitance it charges.

problems.q:
Why does the threshold voltage matter even in the switch model?

A) Threshold sets the logic function

B) Threshold decides whether devices are in series or parallel

C) A switch passing a level its type is poor at stops conducting a threshold short of the rail

D) Threshold only affects leakage, never levels
problems.a: A switch passing a level its type is poor at stops conducting a threshold short of the rail
problems.e: An nMOS passing a 1 turns off when its source reaches VDD minus Vt, so the switch model must be refined to strong and weak levels.

problems.q:
A logic simulator that models transistors as ideal switches is asked about a node driven by neither network. What should it report?

A) The node takes the value of the last input that changed

B) The node is a logic 1

C) The node is a logic 0

D) The node holds its previous value on its capacitance (high impedance)
problems.a: The node holds its previous value on its capacitance (high impedance)
problems.e: With no conducting path the node is undriven; its stored charge keeps the old value for a while. Switch-level simulators track this as a charge-storage state.

label: Static CMOS gate structure
prereqs: Logical equivalence, De Morgan and normal forms
lesson:
# Static CMOS gate structure

Every combinational standard cell in a digital library, from an inverter to an AOI222, is a static CMOS gate: an nMOS pull-down network and a dual pMOS pull-up network sharing one output. Synthesis maps logic onto these cells, extraction recognizes them in layout, and characterization measures them. A tool designer needs to go from a Boolean function to the two networks and back without hesitation, because cell generators, LVS and transistor-level verifiers all perform exactly this translation.

## The pull-down network from the function

A single-stage static CMOS gate computes an inverting function $F = \overline{E}$, where $E$ is built from the inputs with AND and OR. The pull-down network (PDN) must conduct exactly when $F = 0$, that is, when $E = 1$. Build it directly from $E$: every AND becomes nMOS devices in series, every OR becomes nMOS devices in parallel, and each literal is one transistor. For $F = \overline{AB + C}$ the PDN is (A series B) in parallel with C, which we write S(A, B) inside P(...): P(S(A, B), C). Because only un-complemented inputs appear, a function such as an AND or an XOR needs either an extra inverter stage or complemented inputs; a single static stage is always inverting.

## The pull-up network is the dual

The pull-up network (PUN) must conduct exactly when the PDN does not. By De Morgan, $\overline{E}$ in pMOS terms is obtained by exchanging series and parallel at every level of the PDN, keeping the same input on each device. For $F = \overline{AB + C}$, the PDN P(S(A, B), C) becomes the PUN S(P(A, B), C): A and B in parallel, in series with C. Check one vector: A = 1, B = 0, C = 0. The PDN has A on but B and C off, so it does not conduct; in the PUN, B's pMOS is on (gate low) and C's pMOS is on, so the output is pulled high, and indeed $F = \overline{0 + 0} = 1$. The duality must be applied at every level; swapping only the outermost connection is a common error.

## Why the structure is worth its cost

Static CMOS uses two transistors per literal, more than pass-transistor or dynamic styles, yet libraries are built almost entirely from it. The reasons are tool-friendly properties. The output is always driven by one network, so it is restored to a full rail regardless of input slew or noise. There is no static current between the rails apart from leakage. Every input sees only gate capacitance, so a cell's input is a fixed capacitance and its delay depends only on input slew and output load, which is exactly what a Liberty table can capture. And correctness is independent of timing: any input sequence gives the right output once inputs settle, so static timing analysis is sound. These properties are what let a library hide transistors behind arcs.

## Going deeper

Weste and Harris, "CMOS VLSI Design" (4th ed.), sections 1.4 and 9.2; Rabaey, Chandrakasan and Nikolic, "Digital Integrated Circuits" (2nd ed.), chapter 6.

label: Transistor counts and series stacks
prereqs: The product and sum rules for counting
lesson:
# Transistor counts and series stacks

Area, input capacitance and worst-case delay of a static gate all follow from two numbers that can be read straight off its Boolean expression: how many transistors it has, and how tall its tallest series stack is. Cell-library planners use them to decide which complex gates are worth offering, and synthesis cost models use them to estimate area. They also explain why libraries stop at three or four series devices.

## Two transistors per literal

In a single-stage static CMOS gate each literal of the expression drives one nMOS in the pull-down network and one pMOS in the pull-up network. The transistor count is therefore twice the number of literal occurrences. A NAND$n$ or NOR$n$ has $2n$ transistors: a NAND4 has 8. A compound gate such as $\overline{AB + CD + E}$ has 5 literals and so 10 transistors in one stage, where a NAND-and-inverter implementation needs several stages. If a variable appears twice in the expression, it drives two transistors in each network. The count ignores any output inverter: a non-inverting cell such as AND2 is a NAND2 plus an inverter, 6 transistors.

## The tallest series stack

Delay and sizing depend on the longest chain of series devices from the output to a rail. Compute it recursively from the expression. In the pull-down network AND is series and OR is parallel: a series group's height is the sum of its children's heights, a parallel group's height is the largest child's height, and a literal has height 1. For $\overline{(A + B)(C + D)}$ the PDN is two parallel pairs in series, height $1 + 1 = 2$. The pull-up network is the dual, so the roles flip: OR terms are series. For $\overline{AB + C + D}$ the PDN has height 2 (the AB pair), while the PUN puts the three OR terms in series, with AB as a parallel pair, height $1 + 1 + 1 = 3$.

## Why stacks are kept short

A series stack of $n$ devices has $n$ times the resistance of one, so each device must be made $n$ times wider to keep the gate's drive, which multiplies its input capacitance and its internal diffusion. Delay through a stack also grows faster than linearly once internal node capacitances are counted, and the device nearest the output suffers body effect and a reduced gate overdrive. pMOS stacks are worst because holes are slower, so a NOR4 needs pMOS devices about $4\gamma$ wide where $\gamma$ is the pMOS-to-nMOS width ratio of a unit inverter. This is why libraries offer NAND4 but rarely NOR4, and why compound gates are usually limited to stacks of three or four.

## Going deeper

Weste and Harris, "CMOS VLSI Design" (4th ed.), sections 1.4 and 9.2.

label: AOI and OAI compound gates
prereqs: Logical equivalence, De Morgan and normal forms
lesson:
# AOI and OAI compound gates

Compound AND-OR-invert (AOI) and OR-AND-invert (OAI) cells implement a two-level function in one static stage. They are some of the most valuable cells in a library: technology mappers in synthesis tools such as ABC use them to collapse several gates into one, saving area, delay and power. A tool writer must know the naming convention cold, because cell matching, library parsing and equivalence checking all depend on reading a name or a Liberty function correctly.

## Reading the name

An AOI cell ANDs groups of inputs, ORs the group results, and inverts. An OAI cell ORs the groups, ANDs the results, and inverts. The digits after the letters give the group sizes, with 1 meaning a single input that enters the outer operator directly. With inputs lettered in group order:

- AOI21: $F = \overline{AB + C}$.
- AOI22: $F = \overline{AB + CD}$.
- AOI211: $F = \overline{AB + C + D}$.
- OAI21: $F = \overline{(A + B)C}$.
- OAI22: $F = \overline{(A + B)(C + D)}$.

The cells AO21 and OA21, without the I, are the non-inverting versions: the same stage followed by an inverter. A Liberty file states each cell's function explicitly, for example function : "!((A1&A2)|B)", so tools never have to trust the name; but humans and scripts do.

## Inputs, transistors and networks

Because AOI and OAI functions are single-stage static gates, their structure follows the general rules. The number of inputs is the sum of the digits, and the transistor count is twice that: an AOI221 has 5 inputs and 10 transistors. The networks come from the expression: in an AOI22 the pull-down network is two series pairs in parallel, P(S(A, B), S(C, D)), and the pull-up network is the dual, two parallel pairs in series, S(P(A, B), P(C, D)). An OAI is the mirror image: its pull-down has parallel groups in series. A useful symmetry: the pull-up of an AOI has the shape of the pull-down of the corresponding OAI, which is why both families exist with similar areas and why their pMOS stacks set their speed.

## Why mappers love compound cells

Consider $\overline{AB + CD}$. Built from simple gates it is two NAND2s feeding an AND2 (a NAND2 and an inverter): three stages and 14 transistors. As an AOI22 it is one stage of 8 transistors with no internal nodes to route. The single-stage version has a higher logical effort per input than a NAND2 (with a pMOS-to-nMOS ratio of 2, each AOI22 input has $g = 2$), but one stage of delay instead of two or three, and fewer wires for the placer and router. Technology mapping in ABC or Yosys enumerates cuts of the logic network and matches each cut's function against library cells, so compound cells give the mapper more ways to cover a function cheaply.

## Going deeper

Weste and Harris, "CMOS VLSI Design" (4th ed.), section 9.2; Mishchenko, Chatterjee and Brayton, "DAG-aware AIG rewriting" and the ABC documentation on technology mapping.

label: Transmission gates and pass-transistor logic
lesson:
# Transmission gates and pass-transistor logic

A transmission gate is an nMOS and a pMOS in parallel, driven by complementary controls, that passes a signal in either direction without restoring it. It is the workhorse inside library multiplexers, XORs, latches and flip-flops. A tool designer meets it in characterization (internal nodes with no gain), in switch-level and static checks (degraded levels), and in timing (RC chains through switches).

## Strong and weak levels

A single pass transistor is a poor switch for one of the two levels. An nMOS with its gate at $V_{DD}$ passes a 0 perfectly, but when passing a 1 its source rises until $V_{GS}$ falls to $V_{tn}$ and then it turns off: the output settles at $V_{DD} - V_{tn}$. With $V_{DD} = 0.9$ V and $V_{tn} = 0.3$ V that is 0.6 V. Body effect makes it worse, because the rising source raises the threshold. A pMOS with its gate at 0 V passes a strong 1 but a weak 0, stopping at $|V_{tp}|$. Putting both in parallel fixes this: when one device starts to cut off, the other is still fully on, so a transmission gate passes both rails fully. A chain of nMOS pass devices with gates tied to $V_{DD}$ loses only one threshold, not one per stage; drops accumulate only when one pass device's output drives the next device's gate.

## Pass networks in library cells

Transmission gates build compact functions. A 2:1 multiplexer is two transmission gates sharing an output, one controlled by S and one by its complement: four transistors plus an inverter for the select. An XOR can be made from two transmission gates and inverters. Latches use one transmission gate to admit data and another to close a feedback loop. Because a transmission gate has no gain, its output is driven through whatever drives its input. Library cells therefore surround pass networks with restoring inverters at their boundaries, so that each input pin presents a fixed gate capacitance and each output has a defined drive. That buffering is what lets characterization reduce the cell to ordinary pin-to-pin arcs.

## Costs that tools must see

Three effects make pass logic tricky outside a cell. A chain of $n$ transmission gates is an RC ladder whose Elmore delay grows as $n^2$, so long chains need buffers. A weak level, such as $V_{DD} - V_t$ from an nMOS, feeding a static inverter leaves the inverter's pMOS slightly on, wasting static current and eroding the next stage's noise margin. And a transmission gate exposed at a cell pin couples the external driver to internal nodes, so the pin capacitance depends on the state of the cell, breaking the fixed-load abstraction a timer assumes. Static checkers flag weak levels and unbuffered pass gates, and a timer handles internal pass networks only through the characterized arcs of the cell that contains them.

## Going deeper

Weste and Harris, "CMOS VLSI Design" (4th ed.), sections 1.4.6 and 9.2.5; Rabaey, Chandrakasan and Nikolic, "Digital Integrated Circuits" (2nd ed.), section 6.3.

label: The CMOS inverter transfer characteristic
lesson:
# The CMOS inverter transfer characteristic

The voltage transfer characteristic (VTC) of the CMOS inverter, output voltage against input voltage, is the reference curve for every static gate. Its switching threshold sets where a gate decides between 0 and 1, its slope sets noise immunity, and its shape explains why CMOS restores levels. Characterization flows and noise-analysis tools measure points on this curve, and sizing decisions start from it.

## Five regions of the curve

Sweep the input from 0 to $V_{DD}$. Below $V_{tn}$ the nMOS is off and the pMOS pulls the output to $V_{DD}$. Just above $V_{tn}$ the nMOS conducts in saturation while the pMOS stays in its linear region, and the output begins to fall. Near the middle both devices are saturated; in an ideal square-law device this region is almost vertical, so a small input change produces a large output change: the gain is high. Further on, the pMOS saturates while the nMOS enters its linear region, and above $V_{DD} - |V_{tp}|$ the pMOS is off and the output sits at 0. The output stays at a rail over wide input ranges and moves through a steep transition in between. That steep, high-gain middle is what makes a chain of inverters restore a degraded logic level back to a clean rail.

## Computing the switching threshold

The switching threshold $V_M$ is the input voltage at which $V_{out} = V_{in}$. There both devices are saturated, and with the long-channel square law their currents are equal:
$$\frac{k_n}{2}(V_M - V_{tn})^2 = \frac{k_p}{2}(V_{DD} - V_M - |V_{tp}|)^2.$$
Taking square roots with $r = \sqrt{k_p / k_n}$ gives
$$V_M = \frac{V_{tn} + r(V_{DD} - |V_{tp}|)}{1 + r}.$$
Each $k$ is proportional to mobility times $W/L$, so $k_p/k_n = (\mu_p W_p)/(\mu_n W_n)$. Example: $V_{DD} = 1.2$ V, $V_{tn} = |V_{tp}| = 0.4$ V and $k_p = k_n$ give $r = 1$ and $V_M = (0.4 + 0.8)/2 = 0.6$ V, exactly midway. With $W_p = W_n$ and $\mu_n = 2\mu_p$, $r = \sqrt{0.5} = 0.707$ and $V_M = (0.4 + 0.566)/1.707 = 0.566$ V: the stronger nMOS pulls the threshold down.

## Sizing to place the threshold

Inverting the formula gives the strength ratio needed for a target $V_M$: $r = (V_M - V_{tn})/(V_{DD} - V_M - |V_{tp}|)$, then $W_p/W_n = r^2 \mu_n/\mu_p$. For a symmetric threshold with equal thresholds, $r = 1$ and $W_p/W_n = \mu_n/\mu_p$, about 2 to 3 in older planar processes. Two cautions matter for tools. First, short-channel devices are closer to velocity-saturated than square-law, so real current is nearer linear in overdrive and the required ratio is smaller; characterization measures the true curve rather than trusting the formula. Second, $V_M$ is weakly sensitive to sizing: doubling $W_p$ moves it only modestly. That is why libraries size for equal rise and fall delays rather than for an exact $V_M$, and accept wherever the threshold lands.

## Going deeper

Rabaey, Chandrakasan and Nikolic, "Digital Integrated Circuits" (2nd ed.), chapter 5; Weste and Harris, "CMOS VLSI Design" (4th ed.), section 2.5.

problems.q: A long-channel CMOS inverter obeys the square law with $V_{DD} = 1.8$ V, $V_{tn} = 0.3$ V, $|V_{tp}| = 0.4$ V and $k_p / k_n = 4$. At its switching threshold $V_M$ both devices are saturated and carry equal current. What is $V_M$ in volts? Round to 3 decimal places.
problems.e: Equating the saturation currents gives $V_M = (V_{tn} + r(V_{DD} - |V_{tp}|))/(1 + r)$ with $r = \sqrt{k_p/k_n} = 2$. That is 1.033 V.

A long-channel inverter has $W_p / W_n = 2$ with equal lengths, and electron mobility is 2 times hole mobility. With $V_{DD} = 1.8$ V, $V_{tn} = 0.4$ V and $|V_{tp}| = 0.45$ V, what is the switching threshold $V_M$ in volts? Round to 3 decimal places.

You want a long-channel inverter to switch at exactly $V_M = V_{DD}/2$ with $V_{DD} = 1.2$ V, $V_{tn} = 0.3$ V and $|V_{tp}| = 0.4$ V. Electron mobility is 2.5 times hole mobility and the lengths are equal. What width ratio $W_p / W_n$ is required? Round to 2 decimal places.

problems.e: Equal saturation currents at $V_M$ need $r = \sqrt{k_p/k_n} = (V_M - V_{tn})/(V_{DD} - V_M - |V_{tp}|) = 1$. Then $k_p/k_n = r^2 = 1$ and $W_p/W_n = r^2 \mu_n/\mu_p = 2.5$.

problems.q: You want a long-channel inverter to switch at exactly $V_M = V_{DD}/2$ with $V_{DD} = 1$ V, $V_{tn} = 0.45$ V and $|V_{tp}| = 0.3$ V. Electron mobility is 3 times hole mobility and the lengths are equal. What width ratio $W_p / W_n$ is required? Round to 2 decimal places.

label: Noise margins
prereqs: Derivative as slope of tangent line
lesson:
# Noise margins

Noise margins quantify how much a logic level can be disturbed, by crosstalk, supply bounce or leakage, before the receiving gate misreads it. They connect the inverter's transfer curve to the noise and signal-integrity checks that signoff tools run on every net. A designer of those tools needs the exact definitions, and needs to know that a margin belongs to a driver-receiver pair rather than to one gate.

## Defining the four levels

Four voltages define the margins. $V_{OH}$ and $V_{OL}$ are the output levels a driver guarantees for a 1 and a 0, close to $V_{DD}$ and 0 for static CMOS. $V_{IH}$ and $V_{IL}$ are input thresholds of the receiver: any input above $V_{IH}$ is read as 1 and any below $V_{IL}$ as 0. The standard choice puts $V_{IL}$ and $V_{IH}$ at the two points where the VTC slope is -1, the unity-gain points; between them the gate amplifies noise. The margins are
$$NM_H = V_{OH} - V_{IH}, \qquad NM_L = V_{IL} - V_{OL}.$$
With $V_{OH} = 1.19$ V, $V_{OL} = 0.01$ V, $V_{IL} = 0.48$ V and $V_{IH} = 0.70$ V, $NM_H = 490$ mV and $NM_L = 470$ mV.

## Margins from a piecewise-linear VTC

A quick estimate replaces the transition by a straight line through the switching point $(V_M, V_M)$ with slope $-g$, where $g$ is the gain, and treats the corners of that line as $V_{IL}$ and $V_{IH}$. The line meets $V_{DD}$ at $V_{IL} = V_M - (V_{DD} - V_M)/g$ and meets 0 at $V_{IH} = V_M + V_M/g$. With $V_{OH} = V_{DD}$ and $V_{OL} = 0$, $NM_L = V_{IL}$ and $NM_H = V_{DD} - V_{IH}$. Example: $V_{DD} = 1$ V, $V_M = 0.5$ V and $g = 10$ give $V_{IL} = 0.45$ V and $V_{IH} = 0.55$ V, so both margins are 450 mV. Higher gain pushes both margins toward $V_M$ and $V_{DD} - V_M$, which is why a centred threshold and high gain together maximize the smaller margin.

## Margins belong to connections

A margin compares one gate's outputs with another gate's inputs, so it is a property of a connection, not of a single cell. A driver with $V_{OL} = 50$ mV feeding a receiver with $V_{IL} = 380$ mV has $NM_L = 330$ mV, whatever the driver's own thresholds are. This matters when cells from different families, voltages or Vt flavours meet: a weak driver, a skewed receiver, or a signal crossing supply domains can shrink a margin to nothing, which is why level shifters exist. Signoff noise analysis goes further: it estimates the glitch that crosstalk injects on a quiet victim net, given the victim driver's holding resistance, and checks whether the glitch, after propagating through the receiver, exceeds what the receiver tolerates. The static margin is the first-order version of that check.

## Going deeper

label: Dynamic and domino logic
lesson:
# Dynamic and domino logic

Dynamic logic replaces the pMOS pull-up network with a single clocked precharge device and evaluates through the nMOS network alone. It is faster and smaller than static CMOS, and it appears in high-performance datapaths, register files and memory peripheries. It is almost absent from standard-cell flows, and understanding why tells a tool designer exactly what the standard-cell abstraction assumes.

## Precharge and evaluate

A footed dynamic gate has a pMOS from $V_{DD}$ to the output node and an nMOS foot at the bottom of the pull-down network, both driven by the clock. While the clock is low (precharge), the pMOS charges the output to $V_{DD}$ and the foot is off, so no path to ground exists whatever the inputs. When the clock rises (evaluate), the precharge device turns off and the foot turns on; the output discharges if the nMOS network conducts and otherwise floats high on its capacitance. A dynamic NAND3 needs 3 series nMOS, the precharge pMOS and the foot: 5 transistors against 6 for static CMOS. Inputs drive only nMOS devices, so input capacitance and logical effort are lower, and the output makes only a falling transition during evaluation.

## Charge sharing

During evaluation the output node is floating if the pull-down network does not conduct. If some transistors in the stack turn on without completing a path to ground, the output shares its charge with uncharged internal nodes. By charge conservation, an output of capacitance $C_{out}$ precharged to $V_{DD}$ connected to an internal node $C_x$ at 0 V settles at
$$V = V_{DD}\frac{C_{out}}{C_{out} + C_x}.$$
With $C_{out} = 20$ fF, $C_x = 5$ fF and $V_{DD} = 1$ V, the output drops to 0.8 V. If that falls below the switching threshold of the gate it drives, the logic fails, even though the function said the output should stay high. Remedies are precharging internal nodes too, keeping internal capacitance small relative to the output, and adding a keeper.

## Monotonicity, domino and keepers

A dynamic output can fall during evaluation but cannot rise again until the next precharge, so inputs must only rise during evaluation. One dynamic gate cannot feed another directly, because the first output starts high and only falls. Domino logic adds a static inverter after each dynamic node, so every stage's output rises monotonically; the price is that each domino gate is non-inverting. A weak pMOS keeper fed back from the inverter's output holds the dynamic node high against leakage and noise, at the cost of a fight during evaluation. All of this, clock discipline, monotonic inputs, keeper ratios and charge-sharing checks, is outside what a Liberty arc and a static timer capture, which is why standard-cell flows stay with static CMOS.

## Going deeper

Weste and Harris, "CMOS VLSI Design" (4th ed.), section 9.4; Rabaey, Chandrakasan and Nikolic, "Digital Integrated Circuits" (2nd ed.), section 6.3.

problems.q:
Why can one dynamic gate not directly drive another dynamic gate's input in the same clock phase?

A) Dynamic outputs cannot drive any capacitance

B) The first gate's output starts high and only falls, so the second gate would see a falling input and may wrongly discharge

C) The second gate would precharge too early

D) The two clocks would short together
problems.a: The first gate's output starts high and only falls, so the second gate would see a falling input and may wrongly discharge
problems.e: During precharge the first output is high, so at the start of evaluation the second gate's input is high and starts discharging before the first gate settles. Domino logic inserts an inverter to fix this.

problems.q:
Why is a dynamic gate faster than the equivalent static gate?

A) It has no pMOS pull-up network loading its inputs, so its logical effort is lower

B) It has no capacitance on its output

C) Its transistors switch at a higher voltage

D) It uses fewer clock cycles per operation
problems.a: It has no pMOS pull-up network loading its inputs, so its logical effort is lower
problems.e: Each input drives only an nMOS, so input capacitance and logical effort fall, and the output only has to make a falling transition during evaluation.

problems.q:
During evaluation of a dynamic gate, when does the output fall?

A) At every evaluation phase

B) When the pull-down network conducts

C) When the pull-up network conducts

D) When the clock falls
problems.a: When the pull-down network conducts
problems.e: In evaluation the precharge device is off and the foot is on; the output discharges only if the nMOS network finds a path to ground.

problems.q:
A dynamic gate's output node (25 fF) is precharged to $V_{DD} = 1.2$ V. During evaluation the top transistor of the pull-down stack turns on but the bottom one stays off, connecting the output to an internal node of 12 fF that was at 0 V. Assume the two nodes share charge until they equalize. What voltage does the output fall to?

A) 0.811 V

B) 0.389 V

C) 0.624 V

D) 0.6 V
problems.e: Charge is conserved: $C_{out} V_{DD} = (C_{out} + C_x) V$, so $V = 1.2 \cdot 25/(25 + 12) = 0.811$ V. If that falls below the next stage's switching threshold the gate fails.

Assume the two nodes share charge until they equalize. What voltage does the output fall to?

label: RC delay models of a gate
lesson:
# RC delay models of a gate

The RC model replaces each conducting transistor by an effective resistance and each node by a capacitance to ground, so a gate's delay becomes an RC time constant. It is the model behind logical effort, early sizing in synthesis and placement, buffer insertion and every quick delay estimate a tool makes before it has characterized tables. A tool designer must know its numbers, its units and the factor that converts a time constant into a 50% delay.

## Effective resistance and capacitance per unit width

A transistor's drive current is proportional to its width, so its effective on-resistance scales as $1/W$. Take a unit nMOS of width 1 with resistance $R$. A pMOS of the same width is weaker because holes are slower, so its resistance is $\gamma R$ with $\gamma$ around 2 in many processes. Capacitance scales the other way: gate capacitance and drain diffusion capacitance are both proportional to width, often taken as roughly equal per unit width. A gate's output node therefore carries its own diffusion capacitance $C_{par}$ plus the load $C_{load}$ of the wire and the inputs it drives. Doubling a transistor's width halves its resistance and doubles its capacitance, which is the trade-off every sizing algorithm optimizes.

## The delay of a gate driving a load

With one conducting path of resistance $R_{eff}$ discharging or charging the output, the Elmore delay is
$$t = R_{eff}(C_{par} + C_{load}).$$
Units are convenient: one kilohm times one femtofarad is one picosecond. Example: a pull-down of 6 kOhm with 3 fF of parasitic and 17 fF of load gives $6 \times 20 = 120$ ps. Rising and falling edges use different paths: a falling output goes through the nMOS network and a rising one through the pMOS network. An inverter with an nMOS of width 1 and a pMOS of width 3, with $\gamma = 2.5$ and unit resistance 8 kOhm, has a pull-up of $2.5 \times 8 / 3 = 6.67$ kOhm, so a 40 fF total load rises in about 267 ps.

## From time constant to 50% delay

A single RC driven by a step reaches a fraction $1 - e^{-t/RC}$ of its swing at time $t$. The 50% point is at $t = RC \ln 2 \approx 0.69 RC$, and the 10%-to-90% rise time is $RC \ln 9 \approx 2.2 RC$. A model that reports $RC$ as the delay is therefore pessimistic for a single pole by about 1.45 times; in practice the effective resistance is fitted to measured delays so that the constant is absorbed into $R$. The model's real limits are elsewhere: it assumes a step input and a fixed resistance, while real inputs ramp and real transistors change regime during the transition. That is why the RC model is used for optimization and estimation, and characterized lookup tables for signoff.

## Going deeper

Weste and Harris, "CMOS VLSI Design" (4th ed.), sections 4.3 and 4.4; Rabaey, Chandrakasan and Nikolic, "Digital Integrated Circuits" (2nd ed.), section 5.4.

problems.e: The resistance charges both capacitances: $12 \times (2 + 15) = 204$ kOhm fF, and one kOhm times one fF is one ps.

problems.e: The resistance charges both capacitances: $8 \times (4 + 8) = 96$ kOhm fF, and one kOhm times one fF is one ps.

label: Sizing for equal rise and fall
prereqs: RC delay models of a gate
lesson:
# Sizing for equal rise and fall

Libraries size each gate so that its worst-case pull-up and pull-down match the drive of a reference inverter. This makes rise and fall delays comparable, gives every cell a well-defined drive strength, and is the sizing that logical effort is defined against. A cell generator or a transistor-level sizer implements exactly these rules.

## The reference inverter

Let a unit nMOS have resistance $R$ and a pMOS of the same width $\gamma R$. A reference inverter with equal rise and fall resistance uses an nMOS of width 1 and a pMOS of width $\gamma$: both then have resistance $R$. Its input capacitance, in units where a width-1 transistor's gate is 1, is $1 + \gamma$, so 3 for $\gamma = 2$. Every other gate is sized so that, along its worst-case conducting path, the resistance is also $R$ for both edges. Then its rise and fall delays into a given load match the inverter's, and it can be called a 1x gate. Larger drive strengths scale every width by the same factor.

## Series stacks get wider

Devices in series add their resistances, so $n$ devices in series must each be $n$ times wider to total one unit resistance. Devices in parallel are sized for the worst case, which is one device conducting alone, so each keeps the unit width. For a NAND$n$ the nMOS are in series and each gets width $n$; the pMOS are in parallel and each keeps width $\gamma$. For a NOR$n$ the nMOS keep width 1 and each pMOS gets $n\gamma$. With $\gamma = 2$: a NAND3 has nMOS width 3 and pMOS width 2, so each input sees $3 + 2 = 5$; a NOR3 has nMOS width 1 and pMOS width 6, so each input sees $1 + 6 = 7$. The NOR's larger input capacitance is the cost of its pMOS stack.

## Compound gates by longest path

For a general series-parallel gate, size each transistor by the length of the longest series path through it: width equals that length times the unit width (1 for nMOS, $\gamma$ for pMOS). In $\overline{AB + C}$ the pull-down has A and B in series (width 2 each) in parallel with C (width 1). The pull-up has A and B in parallel, in series with C, so every pMOS lies on a path of length 2 and gets width $2\gamma$. With $\gamma = 2$, input A sees $2 + 4 = 6$ and input C sees $1 + 4 = 5$. Inputs of one gate can therefore have different input capacitances and different logical efforts, and Liberty records a separate capacitance for each pin. Sizing can be refined further (for example, unequal widths along a path), but this rule is the textbook standard.

## Going deeper

Weste and Harris, "CMOS VLSI Design" (4th ed.), sections 4.3 and 4.4; Sutherland, Sproull and Harris, "Logical Effort: Designing Fast CMOS Circuits" (1999), chapter 4.

label: Elmore delay of a transistor stack
prereqs: RC delay models of a gate
Sizing for equal rise and fall
lesson:
# Elmore delay of a transistor stack

A series transistor stack is a small RC ladder: every internal node between stacked devices carries diffusion capacitance that must also be discharged. The Elmore delay of the stack shows why tall stacks are slow, why input ordering matters, and what a characterizer is measuring when it reports different delays for different input pins of the same NAND.

## The stack as an RC ladder

Take the pull-down of a NAND$n$: $n$ nMOS in series from the output to ground, each of resistance $R_s$ when on. Number the internal nodes from the ground end, so node $j$ sits above $j$ transistors and has capacitance $C_j$; the output node, above all $n$, has $C_{out}$. When every transistor is on, the stack is an RC chain from the output down to ground, and each node discharges through the resistance between it and ground. That is the same structure as a wire's RC tree, rooted at ground instead of at a driver, so the Elmore formula applies: each capacitance is weighted by the resistance it shares with the path to ground.

## Elmore delay of the falling output

In the worst case every internal node starts charged high, so all of them must be discharged with the output. Node $j$ discharges through $j R_s$ and the output through $n R_s$:
$$T = \sum_{j=1}^{n-1} j R_s C_j + n R_s C_{out}.$$
Example, NAND3 with $R_s = 4$ kOhm, $C_1 = 3$ fF, $C_2 = 2$ fF and $C_{out} = 15$ fF: the internal terms are $4 \cdot 3 + 8 \cdot 2 = 28$ ps and the output term is $12 \cdot 15 = 180$ ps, for 208 ps. If the stack is sized with width $n$ per device, $R_s = R/n$ and the output term is $R C_{out}$, matching an inverter, but the internal terms remain, which is the parasitic delay a tall stack adds.

## Input ordering and pin-dependent delay

Which input arrives last decides which internal nodes are still charged. If the transistor nearest ground switches last, every node above it is still high and the full sum applies. If the transistor nearest the output switches last, all the devices below it are already on, the internal nodes have already discharged, and only the output term remains: the saving is $\sum_j j R_s C_j$. That is why designers place the latest-arriving signal on the device nearest the output, and why a characterized NAND3 has different arc delays from pins A, B and C. Liberty captures this as separate timing arcs per input pin; a synthesis or ECO tool that swaps logically equivalent pins to improve timing is exploiting exactly this asymmetry.

## Going deeper

Weste and Harris, "CMOS VLSI Design" (4th ed.), section 4.3.6; Rabaey, Chandrakasan and Nikolic, "Digital Integrated Circuits" (2nd ed.), section 6.2.

label: Logical effort
prereqs: Sizing for equal rise and fall
RC delay models of a gate
lesson:
# Logical effort

Logical effort measures how much worse a gate is than an inverter at driving a load, purely because of its topology. It turns gate sizing into arithmetic on a few numbers per cell, so it is how designers reason about paths and how many sizing and buffering heuristics in synthesis tools estimate delay before they have tables. Its definition rests on equal-drive sizing.

## Definition by input capacitance

Size a gate so that each input's worst-case pull-up and pull-down resistance equals a reference inverter's. The logical effort $g$ of an input is the ratio of its input capacitance to the inverter's input capacitance at that drive:
$$g = \frac{C_{in,\text{gate}}}{C_{in,\text{inv}}}.$$
Because both gates now drive a load equally well, $g$ says how many times more input capacitance the gate presents for the same output current. Equivalently, it is how much slower the gate is than an inverter at driving the same multiple of its own input capacitance. An inverter has $g = 1$ by definition. Logical effort depends on topology and on $\gamma$, not on the absolute size of the gate, which is why one number per input pin suffices.

## NAND and NOR formulas

With pMOS $\gamma$ times wider than nMOS for equal drive, the reference inverter's input capacitance is $1 + \gamma$. A NAND$n$ input drives an nMOS of width $n$ and a pMOS of width $\gamma$, so
$$g_{\text{NAND}n} = \frac{n + \gamma}{1 + \gamma}.$$
A NOR$n$ input drives an nMOS of width 1 and a pMOS of width $n\gamma$, so
$$g_{\text{NOR}n} = \frac{1 + n\gamma}{1 + \gamma}.$$
For $\gamma = 2$: NAND2 $4/3$, NAND3 $5/3$, NOR2 $5/3$, NOR3 $7/3$. For $\gamma = 3$ the NOR penalty is larger: NOR2 is $7/4 = 1.75$ while NAND2 is $5/4 = 1.25$. This is the quantitative reason libraries favour NAND-based logic and why synthesis tools choose NAND-heavy mappings in timing-critical cones.

## Compound gates and per-pin effort

For a compound gate, size by longest series path and divide each input's capacitance by $1 + \gamma$. With $\gamma = 2$, an AOI21 $\overline{AB + C}$ has nMOS widths 2, 2, 1 and pMOS widths 4, 4, 4, so inputs A and B have $g = 6/3 = 2$ and input C has $g = 5/3$. Different pins of one cell can thus have different logical efforts, and the faster pin should receive the critical signal. Logical effort grows with the number of inputs and with series stacking, which explains why very complex cells stop paying off: their per-input effort climbs faster than the stages they save. The model is linear and fitted at typical slews, so it is a sizing and reasoning tool, not a signoff timer.

## Going deeper

Sutherland, Sproull and Harris, "Logical Effort: Designing Fast CMOS Circuits" (1999), chapters 1 and 4; Weste and Harris, "CMOS VLSI Design" (4th ed.), section 4.5.

label: Parasitic delay
prereqs: Sizing for equal rise and fall
lesson:
# Parasitic delay

A gate's delay has a part that depends on its load and a part that does not. The load-independent part, the parasitic delay, comes from the gate charging its own diffusion capacitance. It is the reason upsizing a gate cannot make it arbitrarily fast and the reason a chain of buffers has an optimal length. Every delay model, from logical effort to a Liberty table's zero-load intercept, contains it.

## Self-loading from output diffusion

Every transistor whose drain touches the output node adds diffusion capacitance there. That capacitance must be charged and discharged through the gate's own resistance, just like the external load. In the RC model, a gate with resistance $R$, output diffusion $C_{par}$ and load $C_L$ has delay $R(C_{par} + C_L)$; the term $R C_{par}$ is present even with no load. If the gate is scaled up by a factor $k$, its resistance becomes $R/k$ and its diffusion $kC_{par}$, so $R C_{par}$ is unchanged: parasitic delay is independent of gate size. In logical-effort units it is written $p$, with the inverter's value $p_{inv}$ close to 1 when diffusion and gate capacitance per unit width are similar.

## Computing p from widths

Normalize to the inverter: with nMOS width 1 and pMOS width $\gamma$, the inverter's output diffusion is proportional to $1 + \gamma$. A gate's parasitic delay is its total output diffusion width divided by $1 + \gamma$, times $p_{inv}$. A NAND$n$ output touches $n$ parallel pMOS of width $\gamma$ and one nMOS of width $n$: total $n\gamma + n = n(1 + \gamma)$, so $p = n\, p_{inv}$. A NOR$n$ output touches $n$ nMOS of width 1 and one pMOS of width $n\gamma$, again $n(1 + \gamma)$, so $p = n\, p_{inv}$. A gate whose output touches nMOS diffusion of total width 3 and pMOS of total width 4, with $\gamma = 2$, has $p = 7/3 \approx 2.33$. These estimates ignore internal stack nodes, which add more.

## Why parasitic delay limits sizing

Stage delay in logical-effort units is $d = gh + p$, with $h$ the electrical effort. When a gate drives a light load, $gh$ is small and $p$ dominates: a NAND3 with $g = 5/3$, $p = 3$ and $h = 1$ spends $3/4.67 = 64\%$ of its delay on its own diffusion. When it drives a heavy load, the effort term dominates and $p$ is minor. Two consequences follow. Upsizing a gate reduces $gh$ (its input grows, so its own $h$ shrinks) but never $p$, so it has diminishing returns. And adding a stage to a path costs at least that stage's $p$, which is what makes the optimal number of stages finite. In Liberty, the parasitic delay appears as the near-zero-load delay at fast input slew.

## Going deeper

Sutherland, Sproull and Harris, "Logical Effort: Designing Fast CMOS Circuits" (1999), chapter 1; Weste and Harris, "CMOS VLSI Design" (4th ed.), section 4.5.

label: Stage delay d = gh + p
lesson:
# Stage delay d = gh + p

The logical-effort stage delay $d = gh + p$ condenses the RC model into one line: a topology term, a load term and a self-loading term. It is the unit of reasoning for sizing, buffering and path design, and it is how a timer-free optimizer estimates delay across thousands of candidate choices in milliseconds.

## The three terms

Write the RC delay of a gate sized $k$ times a reference, driving load $C_{out}$, in units of $\tau = R_{inv} C_{inv}$, the delay of an ideal inverter driving an identical one without parasitics. The result is
$$d = g h + p, \qquad h = \frac{C_{out}}{C_{in}}.$$
Logical effort $g$ captures the topology, electrical effort $h$ (sometimes called fanout) captures how much bigger the load is than the gate's own input, and parasitic delay $p$ captures self-loading. The product $f = gh$ is the stage effort. Because $h$ is a ratio of capacitances, sizing the gate up increases $C_{in}$ and reduces $h$, which is the only knob the gate's own size gives you.

## A worked stage

A NAND2 with $\gamma = 2$ has $g = 4/3$ and $p = 2$. Sized with 4 fF of input capacitance and driving 24 fF, it has $h = 6$, so
$$d = \tfrac{4}{3} \cdot 6 + 2 = 10.$$
If $\tau = 5$ ps, that is 50 ps. A NOR2 in the same position has $g = 5/3$, so $d = 12$, 60 ps: the topology penalty is 2 units of $\tau$. If the NAND2 is instead sized to 8 fF of input, $h = 3$ and $d = 6$, but the gate driving it now sees twice the load. That tension between a gate and its driver is what path-level sizing resolves. Two stages in series simply add: a NAND2 at $h = 3$ followed by an inverter at $h = 4$ gives $(4 + 2) + (4 + 1) = 11$ units.

## What the linear model hides

The stage-delay model is linear in load and has no input-slew term; $g$, $p$ and $\tau$ are fitted to a process at typical slews, often from simulated or characterized delays. It treats rising and falling edges as equal because the gate was sized for equal drive, and it ignores wire resistance. Those approximations are acceptable when choosing sizes and topologies, because errors are similar across choices, but not for signoff. Real tools therefore use logical effort or similar linear models inside optimization loops (gate sizing by Lagrangian relaxation, buffer insertion, early synthesis estimates) and then verify with a timer reading Liberty tables, which are the measured nonlinear version of the same delay versus load relation.

## Going deeper

Sutherland, Sproull and Harris, "Logical Effort: Designing Fast CMOS Circuits" (1999), chapter 1; Weste and Harris, "CMOS VLSI Design" (4th ed.), section 4.5.

label: The FO4 delay as a process yardstick
prereqs: RC delay models of a gate
lesson:
# The FO4 delay as a process yardstick

The fanout-of-four (FO4) delay, an inverter driving four copies of itself, is the standard yardstick of a process's speed. Expressing a cycle time or a path delay in FO4 units removes the process from the comparison: a design with 20 FO4 per cycle is equally aggressive in any node. Library teams quote it, architects plan pipelines with it, and timing tools use it to normalize reports.

## Defining FO4 from stage delay

An inverter has $g = 1$. Driving four identical inverters gives $h = 4$. Its stage delay is
$$d_{FO4} = g h + p_{inv} = 4 + p_{inv},$$
which is 5 in units of $\tau$ when $p_{inv} = 1$. In absolute time, $t_{FO4} = (4 + p_{inv})\tau$. Fanout four is chosen because it is close to the stage effort that minimizes delay in a buffer chain, so an FO4 inverter is a representative well-sized stage. With $\tau = 6$ ps and $p_{inv} = 1$, the FO4 delay is 30 ps.

## Measuring tau from FO4

In practice FO4 is measured, often with a ring oscillator whose stages each drive a fanout of four, and $\tau$ is backed out. If the measured FO4 delay is 25 ps and $p_{inv} = 1.2$, then $\tau = 25/5.2 = 4.81$ ps. That $\tau$, together with the per-gate $g$ and $p$ values, lets a designer estimate any path in the process without running a simulator. Because $p_{inv}$ depends on the ratio of diffusion to gate capacitance, it is also fitted: one sweeps the fanout, plots inverter delay against $h$, reads $\tau$ from the slope and $p_{inv}\tau$ from the intercept. That is a straight-line fit of measured delays, exactly what a characterization flow does on a larger scale.

## Thinking in FO4 units

A cycle time divided by the FO4 delay gives the logic depth available per pipeline stage. A 500 ps clock in a process with a 20 ps FO4 has 25 FO4 per cycle, of which a few go to flop overhead and clock skew. Processors have been designed at roughly 10 to 30 FO4 per cycle, and the number is a meaningful comparison between designs in different nodes because it measures how much logic each stage holds, not how fast the transistors are. For a tool designer, FO4-normalized numbers make QoR comparisons across technologies and corners readable, and an FO4 estimate is a quick sanity check on any timer result: a 3 FO4 path reported at 400 ps in a 20 ps process means something is wrong.

## Going deeper

Weste and Harris, "CMOS VLSI Design" (4th ed.), section 4.4; Sutherland, Sproull and Harris, "Logical Effort: Designing Fast CMOS Circuits" (1999), chapter 1.

label: Path effort and minimum path delay
lesson:
# Path effort and minimum path delay

A path of gates has an optimum: there is a minimum delay, achieved when every stage bears the same effort. Logical effort turns this into closed-form arithmetic on path effort $F = GBH$. It is the theory behind buffer chains, the first estimate any sizer makes, and a clean example of how a product constraint leads to an equal-allocation optimum.

## Path logical, electrical and branching effort

For an $N$-stage path, the path logical effort is the product of the stages' logical efforts, $G = \prod g_i$, and the path electrical effort is $H = C_{out}/C_{in}$, the final load over the first gate's input. Where a stage's output also drives gates off the path, define its branching effort $b = (C_{on} + C_{off})/C_{on}$, and the path branching effort $B = \prod b_i$. The path effort is
$$F = G B H.$$
Example: an inverter, NAND2 and NOR2 path with $\gamma = 2$ has $G = 1 \cdot \tfrac{4}{3} \cdot \tfrac{5}{3} = 2.22$. With a 5 fF input, a 200 fF load and no branching, $H = 40$ and $F = 88.9$. If the first output also drives off-path gates of twice the on-path input capacitance, $b = 3$ and $F = 267$.

## Equal stage effort minimizes delay

The path delay is $D = \sum (g_i h_i) + P$ with $P = \sum p_i$. The product of the stage efforts $f_i = g_i h_i$ is fixed at $F$, because the intermediate capacitances cancel. Minimizing a sum of positive terms whose product is fixed gives equal terms (by the AM-GM inequality, or a Lagrange multiplier), so each stage should bear
$$\hat f = F^{1/N}, \qquad D_{min} = N F^{1/N} + P.$$
For the three-stage example with $F = 88.9$: $\hat f = 4.46$ and $P = 1 + 2 + 2 = 5$, so $D = 13.4 + 5 = 18.4$ units of $\tau$. The minimum is reached by sizing, not by changing gates, so it is the best this topology can do.

## What the optimum assumes

The result assumes a fixed topology, a fixed number of stages, a fixed input capacitance and a known load, and continuous sizes. Real libraries offer discrete drive strengths, wires add fixed capacitance that does not scale with gate size, and branching often varies across a cone. Optimizers therefore use the logical-effort optimum as a starting point or a lower bound, then snap to library sizes and verify with a timer. The equal-effort principle still guides many heuristics, for example in buffer insertion and fanout trees, and it explains a common observation: if one stage in a timing report has a much larger delay than its neighbours, the path is unbalanced and resizing that stage and its driver will usually help.

label: The optimal number of stages
prereqs: Path effort and minimum path delay
Critical points and the first derivative test
lesson:
# The optimal number of stages

When a small gate must drive a large load, adding inverter stages can make the path faster, up to a point. The optimal number of stages balances fewer, harder-working stages against the parasitic delay each extra stage costs. It sets the length of clock and output drivers and the shape of buffer trees that synthesis and physical tools build every day.

## The trade-off in one function

For a chain of $N$ inverters delivering path effort $F$ (here $F = H$, the load over the first input), the delay is
$$D(N) = N F^{1/N} + N p_{inv}.$$
Few stages means a large stage effort $F^{1/N}$; many stages means a small effort but a parasitic delay $p_{inv}$ paid at every stage. With $F = 256$ and $p_{inv} = 1$: $D(2) = 2 \cdot 16 + 2 = 34$, $D(4) = 4 \cdot 4 + 4 = 20$, $D(6) = 6 \cdot 2.52 + 6 = 21.1$. The minimum is near 4 stages. Adding inverters to an existing path is legal only in pairs if the polarity must be preserved, which is a discrete constraint the formula does not see.

## The optimal stage effort

Treat $N$ as continuous and set $dD/dN = 0$. With $\rho = F^{1/N}$ the condition becomes
$$\rho(1 - \ln \rho) + p_{inv} = 0.$$
For $p_{inv} = 0$ the solution is $\rho = e \approx 2.72$; for $p_{inv} = 1$ it is $\rho \approx 3.59$. The best number of stages is then $\hat N = \log_\rho F$. The rule of thumb $\hat N \approx \log_4 F$ uses a stage effort of 4, slightly more than the optimum. With $F = 256$ it gives exactly 4. The delay curve is flat near its minimum: stage efforts anywhere from about 2.4 to 6 stay within roughly 15 percent of the best, so rounding $N$ to a nearby integer, or to an even number for polarity, loses little.

## Choosing the integer and its uses

Because $N$ must be an integer, evaluate $D$ at the integers around $\log_\rho F$ and keep the smallest. For $F = 1000$ with $p_{inv} = 1$, $\log_4 1000 = 4.98$; $D(5) = 5 \cdot 3.98 + 5 = 24.9$ and $D(6) = 6 \cdot 3.16 + 6 = 25.0$, so 5 stages win by a hair. The flatness of the optimum is good news for tools: buffer-insertion and clock-tree algorithms can choose stage counts and sizes from a small library without needing the exact optimum. It also warns against over-buffering. A path with stage efforts of 1.5 has too many stages, and removing a pair of inverters makes it faster; timing optimizers check for exactly this when they consider buffer removal.

## Going deeper

label: Sizing a path at equal stage effort
prereqs: Path effort and minimum path delay
lesson:
# Sizing a path at equal stage effort

Knowing the optimal stage effort is not yet a design: each gate needs a size. Working backward from the load, each gate's input capacitance follows from its logical effort and the stage effort. This back-propagation is the core of analytical gate sizing and a useful mental model for what continuous sizers in synthesis and physical optimization compute.

## The optimal stage effort for the path

Start from the path: gates with logical efforts $g_1, \dots, g_N$, first input $C_{in}$, final load $C_{out}$ and, for simplicity, no branching. Compute $G = \prod g_i$, $H = C_{out}/C_{in}$, $F = GH$ and the stage effort $\hat f = F^{1/N}$. Example: an inverter, NAND2 and NOR2 with $\gamma = 2$, a 4 fF input and a 120 fF load give $G = 2.22$, $H = 30$, $F = 66.7$ and $\hat f = 4.05$. Every stage will bear this effort when sized optimally, so each gate's electrical effort is fixed at $h_i = \hat f / g_i$: the inverter's $h$ is 4.05, the NAND2's 3.04 and the NOR2's 2.43. Gates with larger logical effort get smaller electrical effort.

## Back-propagate input capacitances

Since $\hat f = g_i C_{out,i}/C_{in,i}$, each gate's input capacitance is
$$C_{in,i} = \frac{g_i\, C_{out,i}}{\hat f}.$$
Start at the load and work toward the input. In the example the NOR2 drives 120 fF, so its input is $\tfrac{5}{3} \cdot 120/4.05 = 49.3$ fF. That is the NAND2's load, so the NAND2's input is $\tfrac{4}{3} \cdot 49.3/4.05 = 16.2$ fF. That is the inverter's load, so its input is $1 \cdot 16.2/4.05 = 4.0$ fF, recovering the given first input: a built-in check on the arithmetic. From each input capacitance the transistor widths follow, using the gate's equal-drive ratios.

## From continuous sizes to a real netlist

The back-propagated sizes are continuous, while a library offers a handful of drive strengths such as X1, X2, X4 and X8. A sizer snaps to the nearest available size, then re-evaluates, since snapping one gate changes its driver's load. Branching changes the recursion: a stage's output load includes off-path capacitance, so $C_{in,i} = g_i(C_{on} + C_{off})/\hat f$ where the branching effort is part of $F$. Wire capacitance adds a fixed load that does not scale with gate size, which breaks the clean product structure and is one reason production sizers use numerical optimization, for example Lagrangian relaxation over a timing graph, rather than closed forms. The closed form remains the right first guess and the right sanity check.

## Going deeper

Sutherland, Sproull and Harris, "Logical Effort: Designing Fast CMOS Circuits" (1999), chapters 1 and 2; Chen, Chu and Wong, "Fast and exact simultaneous gate and wire sizing by Lagrangian relaxation" (IEEE TCAD, 1999).

label: Input slew and the limits of the RC model
prereqs: RC delay models of a gate
lesson:
# Input slew and the limits of the RC model

The RC model assumes a step input, but every real input ramps, and a gate's delay depends strongly on how fast its input moves. This single gap is why timing libraries are tables indexed by input slew and why every timer propagates slew alongside arrival time. A tool designer must know how slew enters delay and what that means for propagation.

## Why input slew changes delay

When the input ramps instead of stepping, the pull-down transistor turns on gradually: its current grows as the input climbs past the threshold, while the pull-up is still partly on and fights it. The output therefore starts moving later relative to the input's 50% point and moves more slowly at first. The result is that delay rises with input transition time, roughly linearly over a useful range. A first-order correction adds a fitted fraction of the input slew to the step delay. Measured delay therefore depends on two quantities: input transition time and output load. That is exactly why a Liberty NLDM table has two axes, and why its rows are labelled by input transition.

## Slew propagates along a path

A gate's output transition depends on its own load and drive, and partly on its input slew. That output transition is the next gate's input slew. A timer must therefore compute, for every arc, both a delay and an output slew, and carry the slew forward with the arrival time. Resizing a buffer two stages upstream changes the slew it delivers, which changes the delay of the next gate and its output slew, and so on downstream, so a local change has non-local timing effects. Incremental timers track these dependencies when they update after an ECO. Liberty supports this with paired tables: cell_rise and rise_transition, cell_fall and fall_transition, each indexed by the same input slew and load.

## Edge cases and slew limits

Slew has surprising consequences. With a very slow input and a light load, the output can cross 50% before the input does, giving a negative delay; timers and libraries must accept this. Slow edges increase short-circuit power, because both networks conduct longer, and make the receiving gate more sensitive to noise. Delays outside the characterized slew range are extrapolated and unreliable. Libraries therefore specify a max_transition on pins, and synthesis and placement tools treat transition limits as design rules to be fixed by buffering or upsizing before timing is trusted. When a step-input estimate disagrees badly with SPICE, the usual cause is a weak driver into a small stage, where slew dominates the delay.

## Going deeper

Weste and Harris, "CMOS VLSI Design" (4th ed.), section 4.4.6; the Liberty Reference Manual (Liberty User Guides and Reference Manual Suite), timing group and lookup tables.

label: Dynamic power
prereqs: Expectation of a function of a random variable
lesson:
# Dynamic power

Dynamic power is the energy spent charging and discharging capacitance as signals switch. In most active digital blocks it is the largest power component, and its formula $P = \alpha C V^2 f$ drives the main power-saving techniques: voltage scaling, clock gating and activity reduction. Power-analysis tools compute it net by net from capacitances and switching activity, so a tool designer must know exactly what each factor means.

## Energy per transition

Charging a capacitance $C$ from 0 to $V_{DD}$ through a pull-up draws charge $Q = C V_{DD}$ from the supply, so the supply delivers energy $Q V_{DD} = C V_{DD}^2$. Half of it, $\tfrac{1}{2} C V_{DD}^2$, ends up stored on the capacitor and half is dissipated in the pull-up resistance, whatever that resistance is. When the node later discharges, the stored half is dissipated in the pull-down, and the supply delivers nothing. So a full cycle, one rise and one fall, costs $C V_{DD}^2$ from the supply, all of it drawn at the rising edge. The result does not depend on the transistor sizes or the speed of the transition, only on $C$ and $V_{DD}$.

## The alpha C V squared f formula

Let $\alpha$ be the probability that a node makes a 0-to-1 transition in a clock cycle, $C$ its capacitance and $f$ the clock frequency. Its average power is
$$P = \alpha C V_{DD}^2 f.$$
For a whole block, sum over nodes, or use the total switched capacitance $\alpha C$. Example: 400 pF of total capacitance, $\alpha = 0.1$, $V_{DD} = 0.8$ V and $f = 2$ GHz give $0.1 \times 400\text{ pF} \times 0.64 \times 2\text{ GHz} = 51.2$ mW, since pF times GHz is $10^{-3}$. A clock net toggles every cycle, so its $\alpha$ is 1, which is why clock networks often consume a large share of dynamic power. Some texts define activity as toggles per cycle, counting both edges, and write $\tfrac{1}{2}\alpha C V^2 f$; the two conventions describe the same power, so always check which one a tool or library uses.

## Scaling levers

The formula shows where power can be cut. Voltage is squared, so it is the strongest lever: lowering $V_{DD}$ from 1.0 V to 0.8 V cuts dynamic power by 36% at the same frequency. Because a lower supply also slows gates, frequency usually drops with it, and if $f$ scales in proportion to $V$, power falls roughly as $V^3$: the same change then saves about 49%. Capacitance is reduced by smaller cells and shorter wires, which is why placement quality affects power. Activity is reduced by clock gating (stopping the clock to idle registers), operand isolation and better encoding. Dynamic voltage and frequency scaling exploits the $V^2 f$ dependence at run time. Each lever has a cost elsewhere: delay, area or design complexity.

## Going deeper

Rabaey, Chandrakasan and Nikolic, "Digital Integrated Circuits" (2nd ed.), section 5.5; Chandrakasan, Sheng and Brodersen, "Low-power CMOS digital design" (IEEE JSSC, 1992).

label: Signal probability and activity factors
lesson:
# Signal probability and activity factors

The activity factor is the term in $\alpha C V^2 f$ that a power tool must estimate from the design itself. It is computed either from simulation (counting toggles in a waveform) or by propagating signal probabilities through the logic. The probabilistic method is the one tools use when no simulation exists, and it has known blind spots that a tool designer must understand.

## Signal probabilities through gates

Let $p$ be the probability that a signal is 1 in a cycle. For independent inputs, gate output probabilities follow from the truth table: AND2 gives $p_A p_B$, NAND2 gives $1 - p_A p_B$, OR2 gives $1 - (1 - p_A)(1 - p_B)$, NOR2 gives $(1 - p_A)(1 - p_B)$ and XOR2 gives $p_A(1 - p_B) + p_B(1 - p_A)$. Example: a NAND2 with $p_A = 0.5$ and $p_B = 0.8$ has output probability $1 - 0.4 = 0.6$. Propagating these probabilities through a netlist in topological order gives every node's static probability in one linear pass, which is how vectorless power estimation begins.

## From probability to transition probability

Dynamic power needs the probability of a rising transition, not of being 1. If successive cycles are independent, a node is 0 in one cycle and 1 in the next with probability
$$\alpha = p_0 p_1 = (1 - p)p.$$
This peaks at 0.25 when $p = 0.5$. In the example, $p_1 = 0.6$ gives $\alpha = 0.4 \times 0.6 = 0.24$. If the NAND2 output drives 10 fF at 0.9 V with a 1 GHz clock, its power is $0.24 \times 10 \times 0.81 \times 1 = 1.94$ microwatts, since fF times GHz is $10^{-6}$. A clock has $\alpha = 1$ under this definition, far above any data signal, which is why clock power deserves its own attention.

## Where the estimate goes wrong

Both independence assumptions fail in real logic. Reconvergent fanout makes gate inputs correlated: in $A \cdot \bar A$, independence would predict probability 0.25 instead of 0. Temporal correlation, such as a counter's high bit that changes rarely, makes $(1 - p)p$ wrong even when $p$ is right. And zero-delay probability ignores glitches: unequal path delays make outputs toggle several times per cycle before settling, which can add substantially to power in arithmetic logic. Tools handle these in layers: propagate correlations approximately, or annotate activity from RTL or gate-level simulation (for example through SAIF or VCD files), and use timing-aware simulation to capture glitch power. Knowing which estimate a report used tells you how far to trust it.

## Going deeper

Najm, "A survey of power estimation techniques in VLSI circuits" (IEEE Transactions on VLSI Systems, 1994); Rabaey, Chandrakasan and Nikolic, "Digital Integrated Circuits" (2nd ed.), section 6.2.1.

label: Short-circuit power
prereqs: Input slew and the limits of the RC model
lesson:
# Short-circuit power

During an input transition there is an interval when both the pull-up and pull-down conduct, and current flows straight from the supply to ground. This short-circuit or crowbar power is usually a small part of dynamic power, but it grows quickly with slow edges. It is why libraries measure internal power against input slew, and one reason transition limits exist.

## When both networks conduct

In an inverter the nMOS conducts once the input exceeds $V_{tn}$, and the pMOS until the input exceeds $V_{DD} - |V_{tp}|$. For inputs in between, both are on. As the input ramps through that window, a current spike flows from $V_{DD}$ to ground in addition to the current that charges or discharges the load. The energy lost per transition grows with the time spent in the window, so with the input transition time. If $V_{DD} < V_{tn} + |V_{tp}|$ the window does not exist and there is no short-circuit current at all, which is one minor benefit of very low supply voltages. With a static input, one device is always off and only leakage flows.

## Input slew versus output slew

The crowbar current depends on the voltage across the device that is turning off, and that is set by how fast the output moves. If the output is heavily loaded and moves slowly, then during the input transition the output is still near its starting rail, the turning-off device has little drain-source voltage, and little crowbar current flows. If the output is lightly loaded and fast, the output swings while both devices are on, and crowbar current is larger. The result is that short-circuit energy depends on the ratio of input to output transition times: matched slews keep it a small fraction of switching energy, while a slow input into a fast, lightly loaded gate is the worst case. Doubling the input slew roughly doubles the overlap time.

## How tools account for it

Because short-circuit energy depends on input slew and output load, it cannot be computed from capacitance alone. Characterization measures the total energy drawn from the supply during each transition, subtracts the energy that charges the external load, and records the remainder, which includes crowbar current and internal node charging, in Liberty internal_power tables indexed by input transition and output load. A power tool then looks up that energy per transition and adds the net's switching power separately. In a power report, short-circuit power therefore appears inside internal power, not switching power. Design rules that limit maximum transition keep input edges sharp and keep this component small, which is part of why buffering slow nets saves power as well as time.

## Going deeper

Veendrick, "Short-circuit dissipation of static CMOS circuitry and its impact on the design of buffer circuits" (IEEE JSSC, 1984); Rabaey, Chandrakasan and Nikolic, "Digital Integrated Circuits" (2nd ed.), section 5.5.

label: Leakage power and multi-Vt
lesson:
# Leakage power and multi-Vt

Leakage is the power a circuit burns while doing nothing: current through transistors that are nominally off. In modern processes it can be a large fraction of total power, especially in idle blocks. Libraries offer several threshold-voltage (Vt) flavours of every cell precisely to trade leakage against speed, and power and optimization tools need the exponential law that governs that trade.

## Subthreshold current is exponential in Vt

Below threshold a transistor is not perfectly off: diffusion current flows that depends exponentially on the gate overdrive,
$$I_{sub} \propto 10^{(V_{GS} - V_t)/S},$$
where the subthreshold swing $S$ is the gate voltage change for a tenfold change in current. $S$ is at least about 60 mV per decade at room temperature and typically 70 to 100 mV per decade in real devices. For an off device $V_{GS} = 0$, so its leakage falls by a decade for every $S$ of threshold. Leakage also rises steeply with temperature, both through $S$ and through a falling $V_t$, which is why leakage is analyzed at the hot corner. Other components, gate tunnelling and junction leakage, add to it.

## Leakage ratios between Vt flavours

Two flavours whose thresholds differ by $\Delta V_t$ differ in off-current by
$$\frac{I_{LVT}}{I_{HVT}} = 10^{\Delta V_t / S}.$$
With $\Delta V_t = 100$ mV and $S = 90$ mV per decade the ratio is $10^{1.11} = 12.9$. An SVT device leaking 20 nA becomes about 1.6 nA in a flavour 100 mV higher. A cell's leakage power is its leakage current times $V_{DD}$, summed over its off devices, so a block of a million cells averaging 5 nW each leaks 5 mW. Libraries typically provide several flavours, for example ultra-low, low, standard and high Vt, with identical footprints and pins so that they can be swapped in place.

## DIBL and the cost of speed

Leakage also depends on the drain voltage. Drain-induced barrier lowering reduces the threshold as the drain-source voltage grows, $V_t = V_{t0} - \eta V_{DS}$, so an off device with its full supply across it leaks more. Lowering $V_{DD}$ from 1.0 V to 0.7 V with $\eta = 0.1$ raises the effective threshold by 30 mV, cutting leakage by $10^{30/80} = 2.4$ times at $S = 80$ mV per decade, on top of the lower supply in $P = I V_{DD}$. The other side of the trade is speed: a higher threshold reduces gate overdrive $V_{DD} - V_t$ and so drive current. Every Vt choice is therefore a leakage-versus-delay decision, which is what multi-Vt optimization in synthesis and physical design automates.

## Going deeper

Roy, Mukhopadhyay and Mahmoodi-Meimand, "Leakage current mechanisms and leakage reduction techniques in deep-submicrometer CMOS circuits" (Proceedings of the IEEE, 2003); Rabaey, Chandrakasan and Nikolic, "Digital Integrated Circuits" (2nd ed.), section 5.5.

label: Multi-Vt assignment trade-offs
lesson:
# Multi-Vt assignment trade-offs

A multi-Vt library gives every cell several threshold flavours with identical footprints. Optimizers start with fast, leaky cells where timing demands them and slow, frugal cells elsewhere, then swap cells with spare slack to higher Vt in a leakage-recovery pass. The arithmetic of that trade, leakage saved against delay spent, is what the optimizer evaluates for every candidate swap.

## Mixed-flavour leakage totals

Block leakage is the sum over cells of each cell's leakage. If HVT cells leak $r$ times less than LVT cells, a block with $N_L$ LVT cells of leakage $P_L$ and $N_H$ HVT cells leaks
$$P = N_L P_L + N_H P_L / r.$$
Example: 8,000 LVT cells at 10 nW and 92,000 HVT cells with $r = 10$ give $80 + 92 = 172$ microwatts. The LVT cells are 8% of the count but nearly half the leakage. This skew is typical: a small fraction of fast cells on critical paths dominates leakage, which is why the choice of which cells stay low-Vt matters so much. Real per-cell leakage also depends on the cell type and input state, which libraries record per state.

## Leakage recovery

Leakage recovery swaps cells to a higher Vt wherever the timing slack allows. Swapping $m$ of $N$ LVT cells to HVT saves the fraction
$$\frac{m}{N}\left(1 - \frac{1}{r}\right)$$
of the block's leakage, if all cells leak alike. With $N = 50{,}000$, $m = 35{,}000$ and $r = 10$ the saving is $0.7 \times 0.9 = 63\%$. Because the HVT version of a cell has the same footprint and pin positions, the swap needs no re-placement or re-routing, only an updated timing analysis, which is why recovery is one of the cheapest late-flow optimizations. Footprint-compatible flavours are a library design decision that tools rely on.

## Spending slack on a path

Each swap costs delay. If an HVT gate is $x\%$ slower than its LVT version, a path of $k$ LVT gates of delay $d$ with setup slack $s$ can absorb $\lfloor s / (d x / 100) \rfloor$ swaps, at most $k$. With 12 gates of 20 ps, 50 ps of slack and a 20% penalty, each swap costs 4 ps and 12 swaps fit. But gates are shared: a cell on many paths can only be swapped if every path through it has the slack, so real optimizers order candidates by leakage saved per unit of slack consumed and update timing incrementally as they go. Swapping also affects hold, since slower cells help hold, and it must be checked at all corners, because the delay penalty of HVT grows at low voltage.

## Going deeper

Wei, Roy and others on dual-threshold design, for example "Design and optimization of dual-threshold circuits for low-voltage low-power applications" (IEEE Transactions on VLSI Systems, 1999); the OpenROAD documentation for the repair_timing and leakage-recovery commands.

label: Energy per operation
lesson:
# Energy per operation

Power tells you how fast energy is spent; energy per operation tells you what each computation costs. For battery-powered and throughput-per-watt designs it is the figure that matters, and it reveals a trade-off that power alone hides: slowing down saves dynamic power but lets leakage accumulate per operation.

## Dynamic energy per operation

If each operation switches capacitance $C$ with activity $\alpha$, its dynamic energy is
$$E_{dyn} = \alpha C V_{DD}^2,$$
independent of how long the operation takes. Example: 200 pF with $\alpha = 0.15$ at 0.8 V gives $0.15 \times 200 \times 0.64 = 19.2$ pJ, since pF times volts squared is pJ. Frequency does not appear: running the same operation twice as fast doubles dynamic power but not dynamic energy per operation. Only voltage, capacitance and activity change it, and voltage enters squared, which is why lowering the supply is the main lever for energy efficiency.

## Adding leakage energy

Leakage flows all the time, so each operation also pays leakage power times the cycle time:
$$E_{op} = \alpha C V_{DD}^2 + P_{leak} / f.$$
With the example above, 50 microwatts of leakage at 100 MHz adds $50/100 = 0.5$ pJ, for 19.7 pJ total (microwatts divided by megahertz is picojoules). At 10 MHz the leakage share grows to 5 pJ. The slower the clock, the more leakage energy each operation carries, because the circuit sits idle but powered for longer. This is why low-activity systems power-gate idle blocks instead of merely slowing their clocks.

## The minimum-energy trade-off

Setting the two terms equal gives the frequency below which leakage dominates energy:
$$f^* = \frac{P_{leak}}{\alpha C V_{DD}^2}.$$
For 19.2 pJ and 50 microwatts, $f^* = 2.6$ MHz. Lowering $V_{DD}$ cuts dynamic energy quadratically but slows the circuit, so each operation takes longer and accumulates more leakage energy. Near and below threshold the delay grows exponentially, so leakage energy per operation eventually rises faster than dynamic energy falls: there is a minimum-energy supply voltage, often near or somewhat below the threshold voltage. Energy-optimal design therefore picks voltage, frequency and Vt flavour together, and an energy-aware tool must model both terms rather than optimizing power at a fixed frequency.

## Going deeper

Calhoun, Wang and Chandrakasan, "Modeling and sizing for minimum energy operation in subthreshold circuits" (IEEE JSSC, 2005); Rabaey, Chandrakasan and Nikolic, "Digital Integrated Circuits" (2nd ed.), chapter 5.
