label: Transistor-level latches and flip-flops
lesson:
# Transistor-level latches and flip-flops

Every register in a digital design is a library flip-flop, and every flip-flop is built from latches made of inverters and transmission gates. Its setup time, hold time and clock-to-q are not abstract parameters: they come from specific internal nodes settling. A tool designer who knows the circuit can read a library's sequential arcs, understand why hold can be negative, and see what characterization is searching for.

## The static latch

A latch has two states. When transparent, its output follows its input; when opaque, it holds the last value. A static CMOS latch implements this with an input transmission gate and a feedback loop of two inverters closed by a second transmission gate. A positive-level latch is transparent while the clock is high: the input transmission gate is on and the feedback is open. When the clock falls, the input gate turns off and the feedback gate closes, so the cross-coupled inverters regenerate and hold the value indefinitely. A dynamic latch omits the feedback and stores the value as charge on a node, which is smaller but loses the value to leakage if the clock stops.

## Master-slave flip-flops

An edge-triggered flip-flop is two latches of opposite polarity in series. For a positive-edge flop, the master is transparent while the clock is low and the slave while the clock is high. Before the rising edge the master follows D and the slave holds the old Q. At the edge the master closes, capturing D, and the slave opens, passing the captured value to Q. The flop is never transparent from D to Q, which is what makes it edge-triggered. Library flops buffer the clock internally to make the complementary clocks locally, so the CK pin presents one small fixed capacitance, and they buffer Q so its drive does not depend on the internal nodes. Scan flops add a 2:1 mux on the input selecting functional data or scan data.

## Where setup, hold and clock-to-q come from

Setup time is how long before the edge D must be stable so that the new value has propagated around the master's loop before the input switch closes. Hold time is how long after the edge D must stay stable, because the internal clock reaches the master's input switch later than the CK pin and turns it off gradually. If the internal data path into the master is slower than the internal clock path, the hold requirement can be negative. Clock-to-q is the delay from the edge, through the slave's transparency and the output buffer, to Q. These three numbers trade against each other: data arriving closer to the edge pushes clock-to-q out, which is exactly what characterization measures when it searches for setup and hold.

## Going deeper

Weste and Harris, "CMOS VLSI Design" (4th ed.), chapter 10; Stojanovic and Oklobdzija, "Comparative analysis of master-slave latches and flip-flops for high-performance and low-power systems" (IEEE JSSC, 1999).

label: Characterizing setup, hold and clock-to-q
prereqs: RC delay models of a gate
lesson:
# Characterizing setup, hold and clock-to-q

A flip-flop has no single correct setup time. Its clock-to-q grows smoothly as data arrives closer to the clock edge, until it fails outright. Characterization chooses a criterion that turns that curve into the setup and hold numbers written into Liberty. A tool designer must know the criterion, because it decides how much margin every timing check in the design inherits.

## The push-out curve

Sweep the data-to-clock skew, the time by which D changes before the clock edge, and measure clock-to-q at each point. For large skews clock-to-q is flat at its nominal value. As the skew shrinks, the master has less time to settle and the slave receives a marginal value, so clock-to-q rises: first gently, then steeply, until at some skew the flop captures the wrong value or never resolves. The curve is continuous; there is no physical cliff at which "setup" happens. Characterization therefore needs a rule for where on the curve to draw the line, and the rule must be applied identically to every flop, slew and corner.

## The push-out criterion

A common criterion defines setup time as the smallest skew at which clock-to-q has degraded by no more than a set percentage, often 10%, from its nominal value. If nominal clock-to-q is 50 ps, the limit is 55 ps, and the setup time is the smallest skew whose measured clock-to-q is at most 55 ps. Characterizers search for this point by bisection on the skew, running one transient per probe, which is why constraint characterization costs many more simulations than delay. Hold time is found the same way from the other side, with data changing after the edge. Some flows instead use a pass-fail criterion, the smallest skew at which the correct value is still captured, which gives a smaller, less conservative number with no push-out guard band.

## Why the criterion matters downstream

Setup time and clock-to-q are coupled: data arriving later than the library setup time would still be captured, just with a longer clock-to-q. The total data-to-output delay, skew plus clock-to-q, is smallest at a skew a little inside the push-out region, which is why some high-performance flows characterize at that point. A static timer, though, treats setup and clock-to-q as independent constants, so the library must pick one consistent operating point, and the push-out percentage decides how much hidden margin each check carries. A change of criterion silently shifts every constraint table in the library. That is why a characterization engine treats the criterion as part of its core definition, not as a tunable parameter.

## Going deeper

Stojanovic and Oklobdzija, "Comparative analysis of master-slave latches and flip-flops" (IEEE JSSC, 1999); Srivastava and Roychowdhury, work on interdependent setup and hold characterization; the Liberty Reference Manual, timing constraint groups.

label: Integrated clock-gating cells
lesson:
# Integrated clock-gating cells

The clock has an activity factor of 1 and a large capacitance, so stopping it where registers would hold their values anyway is the single most effective dynamic-power optimization in digital design. Synthesis tools insert clock gates automatically, using a dedicated library cell, the integrated clock gate (ICG). Its circuit explains both why it is glitch-free and why timers apply a special check to its enable.

## Why a plain AND fails

Gating a positive-edge clock with an AND gate, GCLK = CLK AND EN, works only if EN never changes while CLK is high. If EN falls in the middle of a high phase, GCLK is cut short, producing a runt pulse that may or may not clock the flops. If EN rises while CLK is high, GCLK rises in mid-cycle, creating a spurious edge. Because EN comes from logic launched by the same clock, it naturally changes shortly after the rising edge, exactly when CLK is high. An unprotected AND gate would therefore glitch on almost every enable change. The fix must guarantee that EN is stable throughout every high phase of CLK.

## The latch-based ICG

An ICG for positive-edge flops contains a latch transparent while CLK is low, followed by an AND with CLK. While CLK is low the latch passes EN, and the AND output is low anyway. When CLK rises the latch closes and holds EN constant for the whole high phase, so the AND passes either a complete clock pulse or nothing. A test-enable input is usually ORed with EN before the latch so that scan shifting can force the clock on. Liberty marks such a cell with the clock_gating_integrated_cell attribute (for example latch_posedge, or latch_posedge_precontrol with a test pin), which tells synthesis and clock-tree tools what the cell does. The enable path to the latch is timed with a clock-gating setup and hold check, just like a flop's data.

## Where and when gating pays

A clock gate replaces the hold multiplexers in front of a bank of flops: instead of each flop recirculating its value when EN is low, the whole bank's clock stops. That saves the mux area and the clock power of the flops and of the clock-tree branch below the gate. The saving is proportional to the fraction of cycles in which EN is off; a gate whose enable is almost always on saves nothing and costs an ICG. Placing gates higher in the clock tree stops more buffers but requires an enable valid for more flops. Clock-tree synthesis treats ICGs as part of the clock path, balancing their delay against ungated branches, and moving an ICG changes its enable timing check, so gating is decided jointly with the tree.

## Going deeper

Weste and Harris, "CMOS VLSI Design" (4th ed.), section 10.3; the Liberty Reference Manual, clock_gating_integrated_cell; Keating and others, "Low Power Methodology Manual" (2007), chapter on clock gating.

label: Latch regeneration and synchronizer MTBF
lesson:
# Latch regeneration and synchronizer MTBF

When a flop samples an asynchronous signal, data sometimes changes within the tiny window around the clock edge, and the flop's internal latch is left balanced between 0 and 1. How quickly it resolves depends on the latch's regeneration time constant, a transistor-level property. Synchronizer design, and the MTBF numbers that justify it, follow directly from that exponential resolution.

## Regeneration in a cross-coupled latch

A latch's storage loop is two inverters in a ring. Near its balance point, where both nodes sit at the switching threshold, each inverter is a high-gain amplifier. A small voltage difference $\Delta V$ between the nodes is amplified around the loop and grows exponentially, $\Delta V(t) = \Delta V_0 e^{t/\tau}$, where $\tau$ is set by the inverters' transconductance and node capacitance, roughly $C/g_m$. If data arrives so close to the edge that $\Delta V_0$ is tiny, the latch takes a long time to reach a valid logic level. The probability of still being unresolved after time $t$ therefore decays as $e^{-t/\tau}$. A faster process and a larger, well-sized latch both reduce $\tau$.

## The MTBF formula

A synchronizer fails if its first flop is still unresolved when the next stage samples it. With resolution time $t_r$, clock frequency $f_c$, data toggle rate $f_d$ and an effective metastability window $T_w$, the mean time between failures is
$$\text{MTBF} = \frac{e^{t_r/\tau}}{T_w f_c f_d}.$$
Example: $\tau = 15$ ps, $T_w = 20$ ps, $f_c = 1$ GHz, $f_d = 100$ MHz and $t_r = 600$ ps. The rate term is $T_w f_c f_d = 2 \times 10^{6}$ per second, and $t_r/\tau = 40$, so $\log_{10}\text{MTBF} = 40/\ln 10 - \log_{10}(2 \times 10^6) = 17.37 - 6.30 = 11.07$, about $10^{11}$ s, a few thousand years. Taking logs is the practical way to handle these numbers.

## Designing for a target MTBF

Solving for the resolution time gives $t_r = \tau \ln(\text{MTBF} \cdot T_w f_c f_d)$. Because MTBF is exponential in $t_r$, each extra $\tau \ln 10$ of resolution time adds a factor of ten. Adding a third flop to a two-flop synchronizer adds roughly one clock period minus flop overhead to $t_r$: at 1 GHz with 80 ps of overhead and $\tau = 15$ ps, that is $920/(15 \ln 10) = 26.6$ decades. This is why two or three flops suffice for almost any rate, and why synchronizer flops are special library cells with small $\tau$ and are kept close together with no logic between them. Static timing does not analyze metastability; clock-domain-crossing checkers verify the synchronizer structure instead, and $\tau$ and $T_w$ come from transistor-level characterization.

## Going deeper

Ginosar, "Metastability and synchronizers: a tutorial" (IEEE Design and Test, 2011); Weste and Harris, "CMOS VLSI Design" (4th ed.), section 10.6.

problems.q: A synchronizer flop has regeneration time constant $\tau = 26$ ps and metastability window $T_w = 32$ ps. It samples data toggling at 10 MHz with a 2 GHz clock and allows 572 ps of resolution time. With $\text{MTBF} = e^{t_r/\tau}/(T_w f_c f_d)$, what is $\log_{10}$ of the MTBF in seconds? Round to 2 decimal places.

label: Standard-cell layout
lesson:
# Standard-cell layout

A standard cell is a gate laid out on a fixed template: a common height, power rails along the top and bottom, and a width that is a whole number of placement sites. That regularity is what lets a placer treat millions of cells as rectangles in rows and lets a router assume where pins and rails are. Track height, poly pitch and rail sharing are the numbers that tie the transistor world to the placer's grid.

## The template: rails, wells and devices

Every cell in a library shares one height. A VDD rail runs along one horizontal edge and a VSS rail along the other, so when cells abut in a row their rails join into continuous stripes. pMOS devices sit in an n-well on the VDD side and nMOS devices on the VSS side, with gate poly running vertically across both, so an input's nMOS and pMOS share one poly line. Diffusion is shared between neighbouring transistors wherever the netlist allows, which is why cell layout searches for an ordering of transistors that maximizes diffusion sharing (an Euler path through the pull-up and pull-down graphs). In FinFET processes, device widths come in whole fins, so a transistor's strength is quantized.

## Height in tracks, width in poly pitches

Cell height is quoted in tracks: the number of horizontal routing pitches of the lower metal that fit in the height. A 7.5-track library on a 28 nm metal pitch is $7.5 \times 28 = 210$ nm tall. Cell width is quantized by the contacted poly pitch (CPP), the spacing of gate lines: an inverter might be 3 CPP wide and a flip-flop 20 or more. With a 51 nm CPP, a cell 6 CPP wide in that library has area $6 \times 51 \times 210 = 64{,}260$ square nanometres, or 0.0643 square micrometres. Fewer tracks give denser libraries but leave less room for devices and for in-cell routing and pin access, which is a central trade-off in library architecture.

## What the template buys the tools

Because every cell has the same height and rail positions, a placer can model the core as rows of sites and a cell as an integer-width rectangle, and legalization becomes snapping cells to sites without overlaps. Abutting cells share rails automatically, so power routing for standard cells is just connecting the row rails to a grid. Pins sit on known tracks, so a router can find access points from the abstract view without seeing transistors. The cost of regularity is some wasted area inside each cell compared with custom layout, and limited flexibility: a cell that needs more devices than fit in the height must be made wider or built as a double-height cell spanning two rows, which placers must then handle as a special case.

## Going deeper

Weste and Harris, "CMOS VLSI Design" (4th ed.), sections 1.5 and 14.2; Kahng, Lienig, Markov and Hu, "VLSI Physical Design: From Graph Partitioning to Timing Closure" (2nd ed., 2022), chapter 1.

label: The views of a cell library
lesson:
# The views of a cell library

A cell library is not one file. It is a set of views of the same cells, each an abstraction tailored to one class of tool: the layout for manufacturing, a physical abstract for placement and routing, a timing and power model for analysis, a netlist for verification, and a behavioural model for simulation. Knowing which view each tool reads, and what each view drops, is how a tool designer diagnoses most library problems.

## The views and their readers

The full layout, in GDSII or OASIS, holds every polygon on every layer; it is used for streamout, design-rule checking and layout-versus-schematic. The LEF abstract gives each cell's size, site, symmetry, pin shapes and obstructions, plus antenna data; placers and routers read it, along with the technology LEF that defines layers, vias and routing rules. The Liberty file gives timing arcs, lookup tables, pin capacitances, power and logic functions; synthesis, static timing and power analysis read it. A transistor netlist, in CDL or SPICE format, is the reference for LVS and the input to characterization. A Verilog model gives each cell's behaviour for logic simulation.

## What each abstraction drops

Each view keeps only what its tools need. LEF hides the cell interior, keeping pins where the router may connect and obstructions where it may not route, which keeps physical data small and protects the library's layout IP. Liberty hides transistors entirely, reducing each cell to arcs and tables, so a timer can evaluate a cell by lookup instead of simulation. The Verilog model hides electrical behaviour, keeping logic and sometimes timing checks. The site definition in the technology LEF sets the unit slot that cell widths and rows are built from. Because each abstraction is lossy in a different way, no single view can answer every question, and the tools that use them never see each other's views.

## Consistency across views

A library's correctness is mostly about agreement between views. A pin capacitance in Liberty that disagrees with the layout makes every net driving that pin mistimed. A LEF pin smaller than the real metal lets the router connect badly and fail only at final DRC. A Liberty function that disagrees with the transistor netlist makes synthesis and equivalence checking wrong while LVS passes. Every one of these bugs surfaces far from its cause, in a tool that cannot see the view that is wrong. Library teams therefore generate views from a single source where possible and run cross-view checks: Liberty against SPICE, LEF against GDS, functions against netlists. A tool designer debugging odd results should suspect view mismatch early.

## Going deeper

The LEF/DEF Language Reference; the Liberty Reference Manual; Kahng, Lienig, Markov and Hu, "VLSI Physical Design" (2nd ed., 2022), chapter 1.

label: Rows, sites, rails and utilization
prereqs: The views of a cell library
lesson:
# Rows, sites, rails and utilization

Before a placer moves a single cell, the floorplan fixes the placement grid: how many rows fit in the core, how many sites each row holds, where the rails go and what fraction of the sites cells will fill. This arithmetic sets capacity, density targets and power-rail structure, and placers, legalizers and density models all compute it.

## Rows in a core

A core area of height $H$ holds $\lfloor H / h_{row} \rfloor$ complete rows of height $h_{row}$, the library's cell height, stacked from the bottom edge. A 54,100 nm tall core with a 270 nm row height holds $\lfloor 200.37 \rfloor = 200$ rows; the leftover 100 nm is unusable for cells. Floorplanners therefore size cores in whole multiples of the row height. Each row is oriented: in alternate rows cells are flipped vertically (orientation N and FS in LEF/DEF), so that the VSS rail of one row coincides with the VSS rail of the next and the VDD rails likewise.

## Sites, capacity and rails

Each row is divided into sites of the width defined by the library's SITE. A row of width $W$ holds $\lfloor W / w_{site} \rfloor$ sites, and the core holds rows times sites per row. A 40,000 nm wide core with 54 nm sites holds 740 sites per row; with 200 rows that is 148,000 sites. Every cell occupies a whole number of consecutive sites. Because flipped rows share their boundary rails, $N$ rows need $N + 1$ horizontal rails: one at each internal boundary plus one at the top and bottom edges. With 200 rows that is 201 rails, alternating VSS and VDD. These rails are then strapped to the power grid at regular intervals.

## Utilization and why it is not 100%

Utilization is the fraction of sites occupied by cells. If cells fill 99,160 of 148,000 sites, utilization is 67.0%. Designs rarely target more than about 70% to 80% in the core, because the router needs room to reach pins, the timing optimizer needs space to upsize cells and insert buffers, and physical-only cells (taps, endcaps, decaps) take sites too. Placers model this with density targets: global placement spreads cells so that every bin stays below a target density, and the legalizer then snaps them to sites. A utilization number alone hides local hot spots, which is why congestion and density maps per bin matter more than the global figure.

## Going deeper

Kahng, Lienig, Markov and Hu, "VLSI Physical Design" (2nd ed., 2022), chapters 3 and 4; the LEF/DEF Language Reference, ROW and SITE statements.

label: Drive strengths within a cell family
prereqs: RC delay models of a gate
lesson:
# Drive strengths within a cell family

A library offers each function in several drive strengths, such as X1, X2, X4 and X8. Larger sizes drive loads faster but present more input capacitance to their own driver. Choosing a size is the most common timing optimization in synthesis and physical design, and its trade-off is a short RC calculation.

## Scaling within a family

Size Xk of a cell is, to first order, $k$ copies of X1 in parallel: its output resistance is $R_1/k$, and both its input capacitance and its output parasitic capacitance are $k$ times those of X1. Its delay driving a load $C_L$ is
$$t_k = \frac{R_1}{k}(k C_{p1} + C_L) = R_1 C_{p1} + \frac{R_1 C_L}{k}.$$
The first term is the parasitic delay, the same for every size. The second shrinks with $k$. With $R_1 = 8$ kOhm, $C_{p1} = 2$ fF and $C_L = 80$ fF: X1 takes $16 + 640 = 656$ ps, X4 takes $16 + 160 = 176$ ps and X16 takes $16 + 40 = 56$ ps. Logical effort is the same for every size, which is why it is a property of the topology.

## The smallest size that meets a target

A sizer usually wants the smallest cell that meets a delay or slew target, since smaller cells save area, leakage and input load. The delay $t_k$ decreases monotonically with $k$, so scan sizes in increasing order and take the first that meets the target. Continuing the example, a target of 200 ps rejects X1 (656 ps) and X2 (336 ps) and accepts X4 (176 ps). Libraries also give each output a max_capacitance and max_transition limit, and a size that meets delay but exceeds a limit is still rejected. In Liberty terms, each size has its own tables, so a real sizer looks up the actual delays rather than trusting the scaling rule.

## Upsizing loads the driver

Upsizing a cell multiplies its input capacitance, which slows the stage driving it. If the previous stage has resistance $R_0$ and drives a wire of capacitance $C_w$ into the cell, the two-stage delay is
$$T(k) = R_0(C_w + k C_{in1}) + R_1 C_{p1} + \frac{R_1 C_L}{k}.$$
The first term grows with $k$ and the last shrinks, so there is a best size, near $k = \sqrt{R_1 C_L / (R_0 C_{in1})}$ in the continuous case. With $R_0 = 6$ kOhm, $C_{in1} = 2$ fF, $R_1 = 8$ kOhm and $C_L = 80$ fF, the optimum is near $k = 7.3$, so X8 is the best discrete choice. This is logical-effort reasoning in absolute units, and it is why sizers evaluate a change together with its effect on the driver, not in isolation.

## Going deeper

Sutherland, Sproull and Harris, "Logical Effort" (1999), chapter 1; Kahng, Lienig, Markov and Hu, "VLSI Physical Design" (2nd ed., 2022), chapter 8 on gate sizing.

label: Liberty structure: cells, pins and arcs
prereqs: The views of a cell library
lesson:
# Liberty structure: cells, pins and arcs

Liberty is the text format in which a cell library tells synthesis, timing and power tools what each cell does. Its structure, a library header, cells, pins, and timing groups that describe arcs between pins, defines the timing graph a static timer builds. A tool designer writing a Liberty reader or a timer must know exactly what each group and attribute means.

## Cells, pins and timing arcs

A Liberty file opens with a library group whose header sets units (time_unit, capacitive_load_unit, voltage and power units), operating conditions, measurement thresholds and lookup-table templates. Each cell group holds the cell's area, leakage and a pin group per pin. An input pin has a direction and a capacitance. An output pin has a direction, a function attribute such as function : "!(A & B)", and one timing group per arc that ends on it. Each timing group names its start pin with related_pin, so the arc runs from related_pin to the pin that contains it, and carries lookup tables for delay and output transition. A timer turns every timing group into an edge of the timing graph and every pin into a node.

## Timing sense and timing type

Each timing group says how input edges map to output edges with timing_sense. A positive_unate arc can only move the output in the same direction as the input (AND, OR, buffer, a mux data input). A negative_unate arc moves it in the opposite direction (inverter, NAND, NOR, every AOI or OAI input). A non_unate arc can do either, depending on other inputs (XOR, a mux select pin, a full adder's sum). The timing_type attribute says what kind of arc it is: combinational for ordinary delay, rising_edge or falling_edge for clock-to-output delay in sequential cells, and setup_rising, hold_rising and similar for constraint checks. A timer uses timing_sense to decide which output edge, and so which table, follows each input edge; for a non_unate arc it propagates both.

## What the structure hides and assumes

Liberty describes a cell only by its pin-to-pin arcs, so a missing arc is a missing graph edge, and paths through it go silently untimed. Pin capacitance is a single value (or a rise and a fall value), summed into the load of the driving net, so it must match the real layout. State-dependent arcs, written with a when condition such as when : "B", let one input pin carry different tables for different side-input states; a timer either selects by state or takes the worst. Because table entries are bare numbers, a reader that ignores the header's units or its threshold definitions computes wrong delays from correct data. Writing a robust Liberty reader is largely about honouring these conventions consistently.

## Going deeper

The Liberty Reference Manual (Liberty User Guides and Reference Manual Suite); the OpenSTA source, Liberty reader.

lesson:
# Liberty NLDM timing tables

The nonlinear delay model (NLDM) is the classic Liberty timing model: for each arc and output edge, a two-dimensional table of delay and a table of output transition, indexed by input transition and output load. It is the measured, nonlinear replacement for the RC and logical-effort models, and the core lookup every static timer performs millions of times per run.

## Two axes, four tables

An NLDM arc carries cell_rise and cell_fall tables for delay and rise_transition and fall_transition tables for output slew. A lu_table_template names the axes; in the common convention index_1 is the input net transition and index_2 the total output net capacitance. Each table row corresponds to one input transition and each column to one load. Example: index_1 = 10, 30, 90 ps and index_2 = 1, 4, 16 fF, with the row for 30 ps reading 22, 35, 86. At an input transition of 30 ps and a load of 4 fF, the delay is 35 ps. At exactly a grid point, the lookup is just reading the entry; between grid points a timer interpolates, which is taught with timing analysis.

## Choosing the table from the edges

The tables are named for the output edge. For a negative_unate arc, such as an inverter, a rising input produces a falling output, so the delay is read from cell_fall and the output slew from fall_transition. For a positive_unate arc, such as a buffer, a rising input gives a rising output and uses cell_rise. For a non_unate arc both are possible, so the timer computes both. Liberty also distinguishes the transition on the input, which only selects the row, from the transition on the output, which comes from the transition table and is passed on. Mixing up these two, or reading the input edge's table instead of the output edge's, is the most common bug in hand-written lookups.

## Chaining lookups along a path

Delay calculation along a path chains these lookups. Stage 1's input slew and load give its delay and its output transition; that transition becomes stage 2's input slew, which together with stage 2's load gives stage 2's delay, and so on. If inverter U1 receives a rising input of 30 ps transition and drives 4 fF, its cell_fall and fall_transition at (30 ps, 4 fF) might be 35 ps and 28 ps; then U2, an inverter whose output rises, uses its cell_rise at an input transition of 28 ps and its own load. The load each stage sees is the sum of its wire capacitance and the input pin capacitances of its receivers, taken from Liberty. Every delay therefore depends on upstream slews and downstream loads, which is what makes incremental timing non-trivial.

## Going deeper

The Liberty Reference Manual, timing groups and lookup tables; Bhasker and Chadha, "Static Timing Analysis for Nanometer Designs" (2009), chapter 3.

label: What NLDM preserves and abstracts
prereqs: Input slew and the limits of the RC model
lesson:
# What NLDM preserves and abstracts

NLDM reduces a cell to a few numbers per grid point: one delay and one transition for a ramp input into a lumped capacitor. That abstraction made static timing fast and practical, and every one of its approximations is a place where advanced timers add machinery. Knowing exactly what is preserved and what is lost tells a tool designer where errors come from.

## What NLDM keeps and drops

At each grid point NLDM preserves the delay and output transition measured for one stimulus: a ramp input of the given transition time driving a pure capacitance equal to the given load. It drops the input waveform's shape, keeping only one transition number, the output waveform's shape, keeping only delay and slew, and the load's structure, keeping only total capacitance. It also drops the current the cell draws over time and the way the cell's input capacitance changes while it switches. Within those assumptions the table is exact at its grid points and interpolated between them. Everything else is an approximation layered on top by the timer.

## Resistive loads and effective capacitance

Real loads are RC networks: a driver sees the near end of a resistive wire, and the far capacitance is shielded by the wire's resistance. Using total capacitance as the NLDM load overestimates delay at the driver, because the driver's output moves faster than it would into a lumped capacitor of that size. Timers fix this with an effective capacitance: an iteration that finds the single capacitance drawing the same charge as the RC load up to a threshold crossing, looks up the table with it, and then computes the wire delay separately, for example with Elmore or higher-order moment methods. Ceff is itself an approximation, and its error grows as wire resistance rises relative to the driver's resistance, as it does at advanced nodes.

## Waveforms, receivers and the range of validity

Real waveforms are not ramps: they have tails and plateaus, especially through resistive wires and with crosstalk. A single slew number cannot distinguish two waveforms with the same 20%-to-80% time but different shapes, yet they produce different delays in the next stage. The receiving pin's capacitance also varies during switching, through the Miller effect, which a fixed pin capacitance misses. And outside the table's index range the timer must extrapolate, which is why max_transition and max_capacitance limits exist. Current-source models (CCS and ECSM) address the waveform and receiver problems by storing currents or voltage waveforms, and noise views add what signal-integrity analysis needs. NLDM remains the fast default.

## Going deeper

Qian, Pullela and Pillage, "Modeling the effective capacitance for the RC interconnect of CMOS gates" (IEEE TCAD, 1994); Bhasker and Chadha, "Static Timing Analysis for Nanometer Designs" (2009), chapters 3 and 4.

label: CCS and LVF models
lesson:
# CCS and LVF models

Two Liberty extensions carry what NLDM drops. Composite current source (CCS) models store the current a driver delivers as a function of time, so a timer can reconstruct waveforms into any load. Liberty variation format (LVF) stores the statistical spread of every delay, transition and constraint, so a timer can apply on-chip variation per arc rather than with flat margins. Both are now standard at advanced nodes.

## CCS: the driver as a current waveform

A CCS driver model stores, for each input transition and output load on the table grid, the output current waveform over time, sampled as a sequence of points. Given a load, a timer integrates the current to get the output voltage: for a capacitive load, $V(t) = \frac{1}{C}\int_0^t i\,dt$. With current samples held over 5 ps intervals of 40, 60 and 30 microamperes into 10 fF, the charge is $(40 + 60 + 30) \times 5 = 650$ attocoulombs and the output has risen by 65 mV, since aC per fF is mV. Because the timer has the current, it can drive an RC network properly instead of guessing an effective capacitance. CCS receiver models add input capacitances that differ in the early and late parts of a transition. ECSM is a similar approach that stores voltage waveforms.

## LVF: a sigma for every table entry

LVF adds, alongside each NLDM table, tables of the standard deviation of that quantity due to local random variation, on the same grid: for example ocv_sigma_cell_rise beside cell_rise. A timer doing parametric on-chip variation (POCV) uses a late delay of $\mu + n\sigma$ and an early delay of $\mu - n\sigma$ for some number of sigmas $n$. Example: at one grid point cell_rise is 48 ps and its sigma 3 ps; a 3-sigma late delay is $48 + 9 = 57$ ps. Along a path, independent sigmas add in root-sum-square, so a path's spread grows more slowly than its mean, which is why POCV is less pessimistic than flat derating.

## Asymmetric sigmas and what LVF assumes

Delay distributions are skewed, especially at low voltage, so LVF allows separate early and late sigmas, marked with sigma_type early and late. Early delay is $\mu - n\sigma_{early}$ and late delay is $\mu + n\sigma_{late}$; with $\mu = 60$ ps, $\sigma_{early} = 2$ ps, $\sigma_{late} = 3.5$ ps and $n = 3$, the early and late delays are 54 and 70.5 ps, 16.5 ps apart. LVF still assumes that local variation can be summarized by a mean and spread per arc and per grid point, and that variations on different cells are independent, so it does not by itself model correlated global variation, which is handled by corners. It also multiplies characterization cost, because each sigma comes from Monte Carlo or sensitivity-based simulation.

## Going deeper

The Liberty Reference Manual, CCS timing and variation (LVF) sections; Bhasker and Chadha, "Static Timing Analysis for Nanometer Designs" (2009), chapter on advanced timing models.

label: Liberty power and noise views
lesson:
# Liberty power and noise views

Liberty describes power and noise as well as timing. Leakage is given per cell and per input state, internal energy per transition is given in tables like delay, and noise views describe how a cell rejects and propagates glitches. Power-analysis and signal-integrity tools read these groups, so their exact meaning decides whether a power report is right.

## State-dependent leakage

A cell's leakage depends on its input state, because which transistors are off, and with what voltages across them, changes with the inputs. Liberty records this with leakage_power groups carrying a when condition, such as when : "A & !B", and a value, plus an optional default cell_leakage_power. A power tool computes the expected leakage as the probability-weighted sum over states. For a NAND2 with independent inputs, $P(A = 1) = 0.5$ and $P(B = 1) = 0.2$, and state leakages of 4, 10, 12 and 30 nW for AB = 00, 01, 10, 11, the state probabilities are 0.4, 0.1, 0.4 and 0.1, giving $1.6 + 1.0 + 4.8 + 3.0 = 10.4$ nW. Using state probabilities from simulation rather than independence gives a better estimate.

## Internal power tables

For each output pin and related input, an internal_power group stores tables of energy per transition, rise_power and fall_power, indexed like delay tables by input transition and output load. The energy covers what is dissipated inside the cell: short-circuit current and charging of internal nodes. It deliberately excludes charging the external load, which the power tool computes from the net's capacitance. A tool multiplies the looked-up energy by the transition rate: an output rising 200 million times per second at a grid point of 6 fJ per rise contributes $6 \times 200 \times 10^{6}$ fJ per second, which is 1.2 microwatts. Input pins can carry internal power too, for energy drawn when an input switches without changing the output.

## Total pin power and noise views

Total dynamic power of a toggling output is internal plus switching. If an output toggles $r$ times per second (both edges), each toggle costs its internal energy plus $\tfrac{1}{2} C V_{DD}^2$ for the net, since a full cycle of two toggles costs $C V_{DD}^2$. With 5 fJ internal, 12 fF at 0.8 V and 100 million toggles per second: switching energy is 3.84 fJ, total 8.84 fJ per toggle, or 0.884 microwatts. Noise views serve signal integrity: older noise immunity tables give the glitch height and width a pin tolerates, and CCS noise models describe a cell's response to and propagation of glitches, plus its holding resistance when quiet, which crosstalk analysis uses for the victim driver.

## Going deeper

The Liberty Reference Manual, power and noise sections; Rabaey, Chandrakasan and Nikolic, "Digital Integrated Circuits" (2nd ed.), chapter 5.

label: Cell characterization
prereqs: The product and sum rules for counting
lesson:
# Cell characterization

Characterization turns transistor netlists and foundry device models into Liberty: it simulates every arc of every cell at every grid point and corner, measures delays, transitions, constraints, power and capacitances, and writes the tables. It is the bridge between SPICE and every digital tool, and its definitions and cost determine how much a library can be trusted and how fast it can be rebuilt.

## The simulation count

For each cell, the characterizer enumerates arcs from the function and pins, chooses side-input states that sensitize each arc, and runs a transient simulation per grid point and output edge. The count multiplies quickly:
$$N = \text{cells} \times \text{arcs per cell} \times 2 \times n_1 n_2 \times \text{corners}.$$
A library of 400 cells averaging 4 arcs, with 7 by 7 tables, both edges and 9 corners, needs $400 \times 4 \times 2 \times 49 \times 9 = 1{,}411{,}200$ transients for delay alone. Constraint arcs add many more, because each setup or hold value comes from a bisection search with several simulations per point. This is why characterization runs on large compute farms, why libraries are characterized at a limited set of corners, and why faster methods are an active area.

## Measuring delay and transition

Each transient applies an input ramp and records the output. Delay is measured between threshold crossings defined in the library header, typically 50% of the swing on input and output (input_threshold_pct and output_threshold_pct). Transition is measured between lower and upper thresholds, such as 20% and 80% or 10% and 90%. Example: an input ramping from 0 to $V_{DD}$ between 10 and 70 ps crosses 50% at 40 ps; an output falling linearly between 50 and 130 ps crosses 50% at 90 ps, so the delay is 50 ps. That output spends 60% of its 80 ps swing between the 20% and 80% points, so its 20-80 transition is 48 ps. The load is a capacitor at the table's load value, and the input slew is the row's index value.

## Thresholds, derating and conventions

Libraries differ in how they store transitions. Some store the measured threshold-to-threshold time; others store the equivalent full-swing ramp time, the measured time divided by the fraction of the swing between thresholds, with the convention recorded through attributes such as slew_derate_from_library and the threshold percentages. A 30-to-70 measurement of 20 ps corresponds to a full-swing ramp of $20/0.4 = 50$ ps. A tool that applies one convention to a library written in another is off by that factor on every slew, which then propagates through every lookup. Characterization also measures pin capacitances, leakage per state, internal energy and constraints, and its own correctness is verified by comparing selected points against independent SPICE runs.

## Going deeper

The Liberty Reference Manual, library-level threshold and slew attributes; Bhasker and Chadha, "Static Timing Analysis for Nanometer Designs" (2009), chapter 3.

problems.q: A library of 370 cells averages 3 delay arcs per cell. Each arc is characterized for a rising and a falling output on a 8 by 8 grid of input transition and load, at 9 PVT corners, one SPICE transient per point. How many transient simulations is that?

label: PVT corners and library sets
lesson:
# PVT corners and library sets

A library is characterized at one operating point: a process condition, a supply voltage and a temperature (PVT). A design is signed off across a set of such corners, chosen so that every check is bounded by some corner. Knowing which corner stresses which check, and the exceptions such as temperature inversion, is what lets a signoff plan be both safe and affordable.

## Process, voltage and temperature

Process corners capture manufacturing spread of device speed: slow-slow (SS), typical (TT), fast-fast (FF), and skewed corners such as fast nMOS with slow pMOS (FS) and the reverse (SF). Voltage corners cover the supply's tolerance, for example nominal plus and minus some percentage. Temperature corners cover the operating range, such as -40 and 125 degrees Celsius for some products. Each combination is a separate characterization run producing a separate Liberty file: 3 process, 3 voltage and 3 temperature points give 27 libraries before pruning. Interconnect has its own extraction corners (Cworst, Cbest, RCworst, RCbest), which come from parasitic extraction and combine with the device corners.

## Which corner stresses which check

Setup fails on slow paths, so the traditional setup corner is slow process, low voltage and high temperature, where devices are weakest. Hold fails on fast paths, so the traditional hold corner is fast process, high voltage and low temperature. Leakage is worst at fast process, high voltage and high temperature, since leakage grows steeply with temperature. At low supply voltages in advanced nodes, temperature inversion breaks the setup rule: colder devices have higher thresholds, and when gate overdrive is small that effect outweighs the mobility gain, so cells can be slower when cold. Signoff plans therefore check setup at both temperature extremes at low voltage rather than assuming hot is slowest.

## Choosing an affordable corner set

The full product of device corners, extraction corners and design modes is large, and each combination costs a full timing run. Teams choose dominant combinations for each check, guided by experience and by sensitivity studies, and add on-chip variation (OCV derates or LVF) to cover local variation within a corner. Fixes interact across corners: a hold buffer inserted for the fast corner adds delay at the slow corner and eats setup slack, so multi-corner multi-mode optimization evaluates every change at all active corners together. Voltage-scaling library sets, characterized at several supplies, let a timer handle dynamic voltage and frequency scaling designs between characterized points. Every extra corner multiplies characterization cost as well.

## Going deeper

Bhasker and Chadha, "Static Timing Analysis for Nanometer Designs" (2009), chapter on operating conditions; Weste and Harris, "CMOS VLSI Design" (4th ed.), section 7.2 on variation.

problems.q:
Which corner is traditionally worst for hold checks?

A) Typical process at any temperature

B) Slow process, high voltage, low temperature

C) Slow process, low voltage, high temperature

D) Fast process, high voltage, low temperature
problems.a: Fast process, high voltage, low temperature
problems.e: Hold fails when short paths are fast, so the fastest devices and highest drive are the risk.

problems.q:
What does a library's PVT corner fix?

A) The clock period and the input delay

B) Process (device skew), supply voltage and temperature at which the cells were characterized

C) The number of cells in the library

D) The placement density and the routing layers
problems.a: Process (device skew), supply voltage and temperature at which the cells were characterized
problems.e: Each Liberty file is characterized at one operating condition; a flow loads one library per corner it analyzes.

problems.q:
Which corner is traditionally worst for hold checks?

A) Slow process, high voltage, low temperature

B) Slow process, low voltage, high temperature

C) Fast process, high voltage, low temperature

D) Typical process at any temperature
problems.a: Fast process, high voltage, low temperature
problems.e: Hold fails when short paths are fast, so the fastest devices and highest drive are the risk.

problems.q:
What is an FS or SF process corner?

A) A corner with fast wires and slow cells

B) A corner used only for leakage

C) A corner at a fixed frequency

D) A skewed corner in which one device type is fast and the other slow
problems.a: A skewed corner in which one device type is fast and the other slow
problems.e: Skewed corners stress circuits sensitive to nMOS-pMOS balance, such as level shifters, sense amplifiers and duty-cycle-sensitive clock paths.

problems.q:
At low supply voltages in advanced nodes, cells can get slower when they get colder. What is this called and why does it happen?

A) Electromigration: cold wires lose resistance

B) Thermal runaway: cold devices leak more

C) Latch-up: cold substrates conduct

D) Temperature inversion: falling temperature raises the threshold, which outweighs the mobility gain at low overdrive
problems.a: Temperature inversion: falling temperature raises the threshold, which outweighs the mobility gain at low overdrive
problems.e: Mobility rises as temperature falls, speeding devices, but the threshold also rises. When gate overdrive is small, the threshold effect dominates.

problems.q:
At low supply voltages in advanced nodes, cells can get slower when they get colder. What is this called and why does it happen?

A) Latch-up: cold substrates conduct

B) Thermal runaway: cold devices leak more

C) Electromigration: cold wires lose resistance

D) Temperature inversion: falling temperature raises the threshold, which outweighs the mobility gain at low overdrive
problems.a: Temperature inversion: falling temperature raises the threshold, which outweighs the mobility gain at low overdrive
problems.e: Mobility rises as temperature falls, speeding devices, but the threshold also rises. When gate overdrive is small, the threshold effect dominates.

problems.q:
A team characterizes at 3 process, 3 voltage and 3 temperature points. How many PVT libraries exist before any are pruned?

A) 9

B) 27

C) 3

D) 81
problems.e: Every combination is a separate characterization: 3 times 3 times 3.

problems.q:
Why do teams not simply analyze every combination of library and extraction corner?

A) Extraction corners make libraries invalid

B) The count multiplies quickly, so they choose the dominant combinations for each check

C) Timers can only load one library

D) Corners are forbidden by Liberty
problems.a: The count multiplies quickly, so they choose the dominant combinations for each check
problems.e: PVT corners times extraction corners times modes is large. Signoff picks combinations known to bound each check.

problems.q:
A design passes setup at the slow corner but fails hold at the fast corner on the same path. What does fixing hold usually cost?

A) Inserted delay that also slows the path at the slow corner, eating setup margin

B) Nothing at the slow corner

C) A faster clock

D) Removing the capture flop
problems.a: Inserted delay that also slows the path at the slow corner, eating setup margin
problems.e: Hold buffers add delay at every corner, so they must be placed where the slow-corner setup slack can absorb them.

label: Sequential constraint arcs in Liberty
lesson:
# Sequential constraint arcs in Liberty

A flip-flop's Liberty description has delay arcs from the clock to the outputs and constraint arcs from the clock to the data and control inputs. Setup and hold are stored as tables indexed by the data and clock transitions, and a timer turns them into required times. Reading these tables correctly is the link between transistor-level characterization and every setup and hold slack in a report.

## Constraint tables

A setup or hold check is a timing group on the data pin D with related_pin CK and timing_type setup_rising or hold_rising for a rising-edge flop. Its tables, rise_constraint and fall_constraint for a rising or falling D, are indexed by the transitions of the constrained pin (D) and the related pin (CK). Which variable is index_1 is set by the table template, so a reader must check the template rather than assume. Example: index_1 = data transition 10, 30, 90 ps and index_2 = clock transition 10, 40, 160 ps, with the row for 30 ps reading 24, 20, 8. At a 30 ps data transition and a 40 ps clock transition, the setup time is 20 ps. Setup typically grows with data slew and shrinks with clock slew.

## Setup slack from a constraint

The timer uses the looked-up setup time to set the required time at D. For a capture edge one period after launch, with clock latency $L$ at CK, setup $t_{su}$ and data arrival $A$:
$$\text{slack}_{setup} = (T + L - t_{su}) - A.$$
With a 500 ps period, 60 ps of clock latency, a 20 ps setup time and data arriving at 515 ps, the required time is 540 ps and the slack is 25 ps. The clock transition used for the lookup is the slew at the CK pin, so a slow clock tree changes the setup time itself, not just the clock arrival. Clock-to-q delay, from the rising_edge arc on Q, starts the next path.

## Hold slack and other checks

Hold compares the earliest data change with the same clock edge:
$$\text{slack}_{hold} = A_{min} - (L + t_h).$$
With 40 ps of clock latency, a 6 ps hold time and the earliest data change at 58 ps, hold slack is 12 ps. Hold tables can contain negative values, which mean data may change slightly before the edge; a reader must preserve the sign. Beyond setup and hold, flops with asynchronous set or reset have recovery and removal arcs (timing_type recovery_rising, removal_rising), which play the setup and hold roles for the release of the reset, and min_pulse_width constraints on clock and reset pins. All of them come from the characterization searches that found the cell's failure boundaries.

## Going deeper

The Liberty Reference Manual, timing_type constraint values; Bhasker and Chadha, "Static Timing Analysis for Nanometer Designs" (2009), chapters 7 and 8.

problems.q: A flop's Liberty constraint arc from CK (related_pin) to D. Table rise_constraint (timing_type setup_rising): index_1 (data transition, ps) = 10, 40, 160; index_2 (clock transition, ps) = 10, 40, 160. Row data transition = 10: 33, 30, 21. Row data transition = 40: 40, 38, 28. Row data transition = 160: 70, 68, 58. Values are in ps. What setup time applies when D rises with a 160 ps transition and CK a 40 ps transition?
problems.e: index_1 is the data transition and index_2 the clock transition here, so the entry at (160, 40) is 68 ps.

problems.q: A flop's Liberty constraint arc from CK (related_pin) to D. Table rise_constraint (timing_type setup_rising): index_1 (data transition, ps) = 15, 45, 135; index_2 (clock transition, ps) = 20, 60, 180. Row data transition = 15: 20, 15, 1. Row data transition = 45: 24, 20, 5. Row data transition = 135: 38, 33, 19. Values are in ps. What setup time applies when D rises with a 15 ps transition and CK a 20 ps transition?
problems.e: index_1 is the data transition and index_2 the clock transition here, so the entry at (15, 20) is 20 ps.

problems.q: A flop's Liberty constraint arc from CK (related_pin) to D. Table rise_constraint (timing_type setup_rising): index_1 (data transition, ps) = 10, 30, 90; index_2 (clock transition, ps) = 20, 60, 180. Row data transition = 10: 28, 25, 14. Row data transition = 30: 32, 29, 18. Row data transition = 90: 44, 41, 30. Values are in ps. What setup time applies when D rises with a 30 ps transition and CK a 20 ps transition?
problems.e: index_1 is the data transition and index_2 the clock transition here, so the entry at (30, 20) is 32 ps.

problems.q: A flop's Liberty constraint arc from CK (related_pin) to D. Table rise_constraint (timing_type setup_rising): index_1 (data transition, ps) = 5, 15, 45, 135; index_2 (clock transition, ps) = 20, 60, 180. Row data transition = 5: 36, 28, 4. Row data transition = 15: 38, 30, 6. Row data transition = 45: 45, 37, 13. Row data transition = 135: 66, 58, 34. Values are in ps. The clock period is 1050 ps and the capture clock reaches CK 71 ps after the ideal edge, with a 180 ps transition. Rising data arrives at D at 1059 ps (measured from the launching edge) with a 135 ps transition. What is the setup slack, in ps?
problems.e: The setup time from the table is 34 ps. Required time is $1050 + 71 - 34 = 1087$ ps, so slack is $1087 - 1059 = 28$ ps.

Table rise_constraint (timing_type setup_rising): index_1 (data transition, ps) = 10, 40, 160; index_2 (clock transition, ps) = 20, 60, 180. Row data transition = 10: 14, 11, 2. Row data transition = 40: 20, 17, 9. Row data transition = 160: 45, 42, 34. Values are in ps. The clock period is 550 ps and the capture clock reaches CK 22 ps after the ideal edge, with a 20 ps transition. label: Level shifters, isolation and retention cells
lesson:
# Level shifters, isolation and retention cells

Designs with several supply voltages or with blocks that power down need cells that ordinary logic libraries do not provide: level shifters between voltage domains, isolation cells at the outputs of switchable domains, retention flops that keep state through power-down, and always-on buffers. Power-intent tools insert them from a UPF or CPF description, and timing, power and verification tools must recognize each one. Their circuits explain the rules those tools enforce.

## Level shifters

A signal crossing from a low-voltage domain to a higher one cannot drive the receiver directly. A 0.6 V logic high applied to an inverter on a 0.9 V supply gives its pMOS a gate-source voltage of -0.3 V, which may exceed the pMOS threshold, so the pMOS stays partly on: static current flows and the output low is degraded. A low-to-high level shifter uses a cross-coupled pMOS pair on the high supply, with the input and its complement driving nMOS pull-downs, so that the high supply's pMOS devices are switched by the shifter's own nodes. It needs both supplies, and Liberty marks it with is_level_shifter and per-pin related power pins. A high-to-low crossing is easier: an ordinary buffer on the lower supply can accept a higher input, though libraries still provide dedicated cells for clarity and checking.

## Isolation and always-on cells

When a domain is powered down, its outputs float at undefined voltages. A floating input can sit near the switching threshold of the receiving gate, turning on both of its networks and producing unknown logic. An isolation cell, controlled by an isolation enable, clamps such a signal to a defined value, logic 0, logic 1 or the last value latched, while the source is off. It must be powered from a supply that stays on, typically placed in or powered by the receiving domain, or it would turn off exactly when needed. The clamp value is a functional decision: it must be the value the receiver treats as inactive. Always-on buffers serve a related need: they sit inside a switchable region but draw power from a secondary always-on supply pin, so control signals can be routed through a region that may be off.

## Retention flops and power-intent checking

A retention flip-flop adds a shadow latch, powered by the always-on supply, to an ordinary flop. Before power-down a save signal copies the state into the shadow latch; after power-up a restore signal copies it back. This lets a block resume without recomputing state, at the cost of area and always-on leakage, so only state worth keeping is retained. Because these cells change behaviour with supply state, verification goes beyond logic: power-aware simulation corrupts the outputs of off domains, and static power-intent checkers verify that every crossing has the right isolation and level shifting, that control signals come from always-on logic, and that each special cell's supply pins connect to the right nets. Liberty attributes and the power-intent file together make these checks possible.

## Going deeper

IEEE 1801 (Unified Power Format); Keating, Flynn, Aitken, Gibbons and Shi, "Low Power Methodology Manual" (2007).

lesson:
# Power switches and power gating

Power gating cuts a block's leakage by disconnecting it from the supply when it is idle. A network of switch cells, header pMOS devices between the true supply and a virtual supply rail (or footer nMOS devices on ground), is placed across the block. Sizing that network is a resistance and charge calculation that implementation tools perform when they insert and verify switches.

## Switch on-resistance and IR drop

When the block is on, its current flows through the switches, which act as resistors. With $N$ identical switches in parallel, each of on-resistance $R_{on}$, and a block current $I$ shared evenly, the drop across the network is
$$\Delta V = \frac{I R_{on}}{N}.$$
Example: 150 mA through 2,000 switches of 1,200 ohms each gives $150 \times 1200 / 2000 = 90$ mV, since milliamperes times ohms is millivolts. That drop comes straight off the block's effective supply, slowing every cell in it, so it must be included in timing, usually by analyzing the block at its virtual-rail voltage or with IR-drop-aware timing. Current is not shared evenly in practice; switches near current hot spots carry more, which is why switch placement is verified with a power-grid analysis.

## Sizing the switch network

Turning the formula around, the number of switches needed to keep the drop within a budget $\Delta V_{max}$ is
$$N \ge \frac{I R_{on}}{\Delta V_{max}},$$
rounded up. For 150 mA, 1,200 ohms and a 30 mV budget, $N \ge 6000$. More switches mean less drop but more area and more leakage through the switches themselves when off, since an off switch still leaks; the switch device is usually a high-Vt transistor to keep that leakage small. Switches are placed in columns or a checkerboard across the domain so that every cell is near one, and the power grid connects the true supply above to the virtual supply below. This sizing is done per domain, against the peak current the block can draw.

## Rush current and wake-up time

When a gated block turns on, its virtual rail and all its internal capacitance charge from near 0 V. Turning all switches on at once would draw a huge rush current, causing supply droop that can upset neighbouring active blocks. Switch networks are therefore enabled in a daisy chain: a weak first stage charges the rail slowly, and the strong switches turn on later. If the charging current is limited to $I_{max}$, the wake-up time is roughly
$$t = \frac{C V_{DD}}{I_{max}}.$$
With 8 nF of domain capacitance, 0.8 V and a 40 mA limit, $t = 160$ ns. Wake-up latency is the price of limiting rush current, and it sets how often power gating is worth using: a block must stay off long enough for the leakage saved to exceed the energy spent recharging it.

## Going deeper

Keating, Flynn, Aitken, Gibbons and Shi, "Low Power Methodology Manual" (2007), chapters on power gating; IEEE 1801 (Unified Power Format).

label: Tie, filler, tap, endcap and decap cells
lesson:
# Tie, filler, tap, endcap and decap cells

Some library cells have no logic function at all, or only a constant one: tie cells, fillers, well taps, endcaps, decoupling capacitors and spare cells. They exist because manufacturing, reliability and power integrity need things that logic does not. Placement, routing and signoff tools insert them at fixed stages of the flow and must know to exclude them from logic checks.

## Tie cells, fillers and spares

A constant input is driven by a tie-high or tie-low cell rather than wired straight to a rail. The tie cell connects the gate through a transistor, isolating the gate oxide from rail noise and electrostatic events, and it gives the netlist an ordinary driven net that tools can treat uniformly. Filler cells fill empty sites after placement and routing so that the n-well, implants and power rails stay continuous along each row; they have no logic. Spare cells are unused gates sprinkled across the die in advance, so that a later engineering change can be implemented by changing only metal masks; some libraries offer programmable gate-array fillers whose uncommitted transistors metal changes can wire into simple gates.

## Decoupling capacitance

When many cells switch together, they draw a burst of current that the power grid, with its resistance and inductance, cannot supply instantly, so the local supply droops. A decap cell is a capacitor between VDD and VSS, usually a transistor's gate oxide, placed near switching logic to supply that charge. If a cluster draws an extra $I$ for a time $\Delta t$ and the droop must stay below $\Delta V$, the decap must hold charge $I \Delta t$ while losing only $\Delta V$:
$$C = \frac{I \Delta t}{\Delta V}.$$
With 20 mA for 100 ps and a 40 mV budget, $C = 20 \times 100 / 40 = 50$ pF, since mA times ps over mV is pF. Decap costs area and gate leakage, so it is placed where power analysis shows droop, often as filler-replacement cells in gaps near hot spots.

## Taps, endcaps and flow placement

In tapless libraries, cells have no well or substrate contacts, so well-tap cells tie the n-well to VDD and the substrate to VSS at a maximum spacing set by latch-up rules. Taps are therefore inserted in a regular pattern before standard-cell placement, and the placer works around them. Endcap (boundary) cells terminate every row and surround blockages, satisfying rules on well and poly termination at row ends. The flow order is fixed: endcaps and taps after floorplanning, logic placement and routing, then fillers and decap fillers in the remaining gaps. Logic-equivalence checks and timing ignore physical-only cells (fillers, taps, endcaps, decaps), while tie cells, which carry constants, stay in the logical netlist.

## Going deeper

Kahng, Lienig, Markov and Hu, "VLSI Physical Design" (2nd ed., 2022), chapter on physical design flow; the OpenROAD documentation for tapcell and filler insertion.

label: Characterization as an agent skill
lesson:
# Characterization as an agent skill

Characterization is a natural first target for agent-driven engineering: it is compute-heavy, rule-bound and full of library-specific choices, and its outputs can be checked against SPICE. Packaging a characterizer as a skill, with a fixed measurement core, pluggable strategies, configuration and golden tests, is what lets an agent tune it safely for a new library without rewriting the parts that define what a Liberty number means.

## The four layers of a characterizer

Split the characterization engine as the four-layer model prescribes. The immutable core holds what defines correctness: deck generation from netlist and models, the measurement definitions (threshold crossings, the setup push-out criterion) and the Liberty writer. The strategy layer holds interchangeable policies: how to search for setup and hold (bisection, or a model-guided search), how to choose sensitizing side-input states, how to schedule simulations. The parameter layer holds per-library values: index grids, thresholds, corner lists, tolerances. Observation hooks report per-arc progress, convergence and measurement failures as runs complete. A request to change grid sizes then never touches code, and a new search policy never touches the definitions.

## Change tiers for library requests

Each customer request lands at the smallest safe tier. A change from 7 by 7 to 9 by 9 tables, a new corner, or different transition thresholds is Tier 1, configuration only. A constraint search that reuses neighbouring corners' results as starting guesses is Tier 2, a plug-in at the search extension point; it changes cost, not definitions, and must reproduce the same numbers within tolerance. A change to the setup criterion, from a 10% push-out to a pass-fail boundary, is Tier 3 even though the edit is one line, because it changes what every constraint value in the library means and shifts every downstream slack. The skill's manifest should say exactly which parameters are tunable and which definitions are fixed, so an agent selecting and configuring the skill never needs to read its source.

## The harness and its evidence

An agent editing the skill works inside the harness loop: propose a small change, build incrementally, run the golden tests, compare the produced library against a baseline, feed failures back, and present a passing change as a diff for human review. For a characterizer the golden tests are fixed cells, stimuli and expected tables checked against trusted SPICE within tolerance, and the baseline comparison is differential: every table of every cell, not only the goldens. A plug-in that is three times faster and passes the goldens but shifts one cell's hold table by 4 ps must be blocked until the shift is explained. Runs execute in a sandbox with no network, because foundry models and customer netlists are protected IP that must not leave the site.

## Going deeper

The agent-first EDA material in this curriculum (four-layer engine model, change tiers, harness loop); the Liberty Reference Manual for the quantities a characterizer must preserve.

problems.e: An agent selects by reading manifests, not source: capability, interface and tunable surface are what it needs.

label: Golden SPICE checks for library tables
lesson:
# Golden SPICE checks for library tables

A golden SPICE check is the test that decides whether a characterization change is allowed to ship. It compares a candidate's Liberty tables with tables produced by a trusted reference flow, entry by entry, against a tolerance. Getting the error metric and the tolerance right decides whether the check catches real regressions without drowning the harness in false alarms.

## Relative error at a grid point

The basic metric is the relative error of a candidate value $c$ against the golden value $g$:
$$e = \frac{|c - g|}{g} \times 100\%.$$
A candidate delay of 52 ps where the golden SPICE value is 50 ps has $e = 4\%$. Relative error is natural for delays that span orders of magnitude across a table, from a few picoseconds at small loads to hundreds at large ones. The check runs on every arc, edge, table type and grid point of the golden cells, and for transitions, constraints, capacitances and power as well as delay, because a characterizer can be right on delay and wrong on slew, and slew propagates.

## Maximum error over a table

A table passes or fails on its worst entry, so the summary statistic is the maximum relative error over the grid, not the mean. A mean can hide one bad corner of the table, and that corner, often the smallest load or the fastest slew, may be exactly where real paths operate. Small golden values amplify fixed absolute errors: 1 ps of error on a 10 ps entry is 10%, while on a 200 ps entry it is 0.5%. A report that lists the maximum and where it occurs, by row and column, tells the engineer or the agent whether the problem is a measurement threshold, an interpolation region or a convergence failure in a few simulations.

## Tolerances with an absolute floor

A pure relative tolerance fails tiny entries for errors no timer would notice, while a pure absolute tolerance is too loose for large ones. Practical checks combine them: an entry passes if
$$|c - g| \le \max(r \cdot g,\ a),$$
for a relative tolerance $r$ and an absolute floor $a$. With $r = 2\%$ and $a = 1$ ps, a 12 ps entry may be off by 1 ps and a 150 ps entry by 3 ps. The check is a gate in the skill flywheel: nothing is promoted without it, and its own definition must be versioned, since loosening a tolerance is itself a change that can hide regressions. It complements a differential check against the previous library, which catches changes in cells the goldens do not cover.

## Going deeper

The agent-first EDA material in this curriculum (golden and differential testing); the Liberty Reference Manual.

label: Fast characterization surrogates
prereqs: Fast and accurate engines in a modeling loop
lesson:
# Fast characterization surrogates

Full characterization of a new corner or a new cell variant costs millions of SPICE transients. A fast surrogate, a regression or learned model that predicts tables from a few simulations and from related corners, can produce candidate tables in a fraction of the time. Used inside a fast-versus-accurate loop, it decides where SPICE must still run. Used carelessly, it writes confident wrong numbers into a library.

## What the fast engine trades away

A surrogate replaces simulation at most grid points with prediction: it interpolates between characterized voltages or temperatures, fits smooth delay surfaces from a sparse set of points, or uses a learned model of delay against device parameters, slew and load. It trades guaranteed accuracy for speed. That is acceptable for exploration, for example ranking library variants or estimating a new corner early, but signoff numbers must be traceable to accurate simulation within the agreed tolerance. A surrogate is only safe in an agent loop if it reports a calibrated uncertainty for each prediction, so the loop can decide which values to trust.

## Recursing to the accurate engine

The loop uses the uncertainty directly: accept a prediction whose standard deviation is below a threshold, and send every other point to SPICE. If a table's predictions carry standard deviations of 1.2, 3.5, 0.8, 4.1 and 2.0 ps and the threshold is 3 ps, two points are re-simulated and three accepted. The accurate results then refine the surrogate for the next table. The value of the surrogate is measured end to end: total simulations, including the re-simulations it triggers, needed to reach tables that pass the golden check. A surrogate that sends most points back to SPICE saves little, and one that never does is suspicious.

## Where surrogates fail

Surrogates fail most when extrapolating: a model trained on 0.7 to 0.9 V corners asked for 0.55 V meets near-threshold behaviour it has never seen. A process revision that shifts thresholds changes the training distribution, so the model must be recalibrated with fresh SPICE data. Constraint tables are harder than delay tables, because setup and hold come from searches over a sharp pass-fail boundary, where small model errors move the answer. Transition errors matter as much as delay errors because slew propagates. Most dangerous is miscalibration: small claimed uncertainty with large real error. Spot checks at table corners, high-curvature regions and low-confidence points are the defence, and a failed spot check must widen the recursion to SPICE.

## Going deeper

The agent-first EDA material in this curriculum (fast and accurate engines in a modeling loop); Rasmussen and Williams, "Gaussian Processes for Machine Learning" (2006) for calibrated predictive uncertainty.

problems.a: A calibrated uncertainty estimate for each predicted value
problems.e: Calibrated uncertainty lets the loop decide which points to trust and which to send to SPICE.

label: Agents choosing cell architectures in DTCO
prereqs: Drive strengths within a cell family
lesson:
# Agents choosing cell architectures in DTCO

Design-technology co-optimization (DTCO) chooses the cell architecture, track height, fins or sheets per device, pin layers and similar template parameters, jointly with the process. Each candidate must be laid out, characterized and pushed through place and route on benchmark blocks before it can be judged, so exploration is expensive. Agents that choose the next experiment and run the engines as tools make that exploration faster, and the hard part is scoring candidates honestly.

## The architecture choice and its scoring

A cell architecture fixes every cell's layout template: fewer tracks give density but fewer fins per device and less room for in-cell routing and pin access; more tracks give drive and routability at the cost of area. A candidate cannot be scored on single cells, because an area win can be lost to routing congestion and pin-access failures once real nets are routed. The agent's loop is therefore the harness loop applied to exploration: propose an architecture, generate and characterize cells, run place and route on benchmark blocks through typed tool interfaces, read structured QoR results, compare against a baseline, and choose the next candidate. Because each evaluation costs hours, the choice of the next candidate matters, and Bayesian optimization is a natural method.

## Pareto sets, not single winners

Area, delay and power trade against each other, so the output of exploration is a Pareto set: the candidates not dominated by any other. A candidate dominates another if it is at least as good on every metric and strictly better on one. Given candidates scored as (area, delay) of (20, 18), (16, 24), (22, 17), (21, 19) and (16, 22), the point (21, 19) is dominated by (20, 18) and (16, 24) by (16, 22), leaving three Pareto-optimal candidates. Product goals then select from the set: a mobile part weights power and area, a server part weights delay. The agent's job is to map the front accurately; the commitment to one architecture, which every later design inherits, remains a human decision.

## Proxies and the danger of overfitting

Fast proxies, such as cell area and FO4 delay, let the agent prune candidates cheaply, but they miss pin access, routability and wire load, which only appear after routing. An architecture can also overfit: an 8% area gain on one benchmark, at one corner and one utilization, may vanish elsewhere. Robust evaluation spans several benchmarks, corners and utilizations, and treats a reward measured on a narrow setting as an invitation to gaming. Exposing the engines as tools with typed inputs and outputs, rather than scraping logs, keeps experiments reproducible and comparable, which is what lets a model learn from many runs which architectures to try next.

## Going deeper

The agent-first EDA material in this curriculum (harness loop, engines as tools, design-space exploration); published DTCO studies of track-height scaling in IEDM and VLSI Symposium proceedings.

label: Tool-grounded rewards for library agents
prereqs: Golden SPICE checks for library tables
lesson:
# Tool-grounded rewards for library agents

Reinforcement learning with tools as judges, tool-grounded RL, is how a model can learn to configure and run characterization: deterministic simulators score its output against ground truth and that score is the reward. Library work is a good test case because accuracy is checkable and cost is measurable, and a bad test case because there are many ways to look accurate while being wrong. Designing the reward is the engineering problem.

## A tool-grounded reward

A sound reward for a characterization policy combines accuracy and cost, both computed by tools. Accuracy is agreement of the produced tables with golden SPICE within tolerance, scored as the fraction of entries passing or a penalty on the maximum error. Cost is the number of SPICE simulations used, or compute time. Without the cost term, the best policy simulates everything, which is accurate but pointless; without the accuracy term, it simulates nothing. The scoring tools must be deterministic and versioned, so that a change in reward reflects a change in the policy, not drift in the judges. Evaluation must use ground truth the policy cannot see while acting.

## How the reward gets hacked

A policy optimizes the reward it is given, not the intent behind it. If accuracy is checked only at the golden grid points, it learns to be accurate there and careless elsewhere. If error is measured at grid points of the table it writes, it learns to narrow the table's index range so every point is easy, and real slews and loads then fall outside the table and are extrapolated: the reward rises while timing accuracy falls. If golden cells are recognizable by name, it learns to treat them specially. If only absolute error is penalized, it may settle on a small systematic optimism, which passes per-entry checks but accumulates along paths and hides real setup violations.

## Closing the gap to signoff

Defences mirror the hacks. Use held-out cells and randomized grid points the policy cannot anticipate, rename and perturb test cells, add a signed-bias term so systematic optimism is penalized, and require coverage of the slew and load ranges real designs need. Then measure what actually matters: time a set of reference designs with the produced library and with a fully SPICE-characterized one, and compare slacks path by path. Per-point table error is a fast proxy; differential slack on real designs is the signoff-grade measure, and the gap between the two is where reward hacking hides. A policy is ready only when both are good.

## Going deeper

The agent-first EDA material in this curriculum (tool-grounded reinforcement learning, benchmarks for agentic EDA); Amodei and others, "Concrete Problems in AI Safety" (2016), on reward hacking.

C) Timing a set of reference designs with its library and comparing slacks with the SPICE-characterized library

D) A generic coding benchmark score
problems.a: Timing a set of reference designs with its library and comparing slacks with the SPICE-characterized library
problems.e: The real objective is correct timing on designs, so a differential slack comparison is the end-to-end test.

problems.q:
Why must the reward tools themselves be deterministic and versioned?

A) So the reward can be edited by the model

B) So a reward change can be traced to the policy and not to drift in the scoring tools

C) So the model can predict the reward

D) So training is faster
problems.a: So a reward change can be traced to the policy and not to drift in the scoring tools
problems.e: If the scorer changes, reward improvements stop meaning anything; pinned tool versions make the signal trustworthy.

problems.q:
What is the gap between the fast-proxy reward and signoff quality for a library model?

A) The proxy is always more pessimistic

B) There is no gap if the proxy is SPICE

C) Signoff only reads cell areas

D) Table error at sampled points does not guarantee correct path timing on real designs
problems.a: Table error at sampled points does not guarantee correct path timing on real designs
problems.e: Path-level timing depends on slews, loads and correlations the per-point proxy does not fully capture, so final evaluation runs real designs through a timer.
